title: 3 Weeks in Japan: The Extended Itinerary
content:
Three weeks in Japan is a rare gift — enough to cover the classic highlights and venture well off the standard trail into mountain towns, sacred sites, and regions most first-timers never reach at all. Here's how to think about an extended trip without it becoming an exhausting, sprawling checklist that leaves you as tired as you were before you left.

The strategy for a long trip

With 21 days, the temptation is to add destinations endlessly, turning the itinerary into a checklist that spans the entire country — resist it. The better approach is to do the classic route at a relaxed pace, then add a few deeper regions with real time in each, plus genuine rest days built in rather than treated as wasted time. Quality of experience beats quantity of cities almost every time on a trip this long; three unhurried regions beat eight rushed ones. Use the Shinkansen and luggage forwarding to move efficiently between a handful of well-chosen bases, and resist the pull to add "just one more stop" once your route is already set.

Week 1: Tokyo and the east

Four to five days in Tokyo with day trips (Hakone for Mt Fuji and onsen, plus Nikko or Kamakura), exploring the city's neighborhoods in real depth rather than rushing the icons — a full afternoon in Shimokitazawa or Yanaka, say, rather than a photo stop. Time to enjoy the food scene properly, from depachika basement food halls to a proper izakaya crawl, at a slower pace than a short trip ever allows.

Week 2: Central Japan and Kansai

Head into central Japan on the way west: the traditional Edo-period streets of Takayama and the thatched-roof villages of the Japan Alps, and the refined gardens and culture of Kanazawa, home to Kenroku-en, one of Japan's three great gardens. Then settle into Kyoto for several unhurried days (temples, Gion, Arashiyama), with day trips to Nara and Osaka — with this much time, you can actually let a rainy afternoon become a museum day instead of a crisis.

Week 3: West and beyond

Continue west to Hiroshima and Miyajima (the Peace Park and the torii gate that floats at high tide). With remaining time, choose a deeper detour based on your interests:

  • Koyasan — temple lodging (shukubo), morning meditation, and the vast, moss-covered Okunoin cemetery on a sacred mountain.
  • The Kii Peninsula — ancient Kumano Kodo pilgrimage trails and remote onsen villages, genuinely far from the usual tourist track.
  • Kyushu — the southern island, with the hot-spring capital of Beppu, active volcanoes, and Fukuoka's renowned food scene.
  • Hokkaido — the northern island, for national-park wilderness, seafood and dairy, and (in winter) some of the best powder skiing on earth around Niseko.
  • The Japan Sea coast or Tohoku — rural, scenic, and barely touristed by international visitors even in peak season.

Build in rest

Three weeks of nonstop sightseeing will wear anyone down, no matter how much you love Japan. Deliberately schedule slower days: a second day in a place you love, an onsen-town stay where you do nothing but soak and eat kaiseki, or an unstructured day to wander a neighborhood with no itinerary at all. These often become the most memorable parts of a long trip, precisely because nothing about them was planned.

Tips

  • The JR Pass is most likely worth it on a trip like this — a 21-day nationwide pass runs around ¥100,000, and with this much long-distance travel across Tokyo, central Japan, Kansai, and Hiroshima (plus whatever western detour you add), the fares for equivalent point-to-point tickets can genuinely exceed that. Still price it against your specific planned Shinkansen fares before buying, since the answer always depends on your exact route — that pricing decision is exactly the kind of thing Japan, Worked Out is built to walk through in detail.
  • Luggage forwarding (takkyubin) between bases is invaluable over three weeks — send bags ahead a day and travel light on transit days instead of hauling everything through train stations.
  • Don't change hotels more than necessary; use day trips from a few well-placed bases rather than a new hotel every two nights.
  • Mix the famous and the obscure — the contrast between a crowded icon and a quiet backstreet is part of what keeps a long trip feeling fresh rather than repetitive.
  • Vary your accommodation: city hotels, a ryokan, a temple stay, an onsen inn — each is a genuinely different experience, not just a place to sleep.

Bottom line

Three weeks lets you go beyond the postcard Japan into its mountains, sacred sites, and quieter regions — but the secret is restraint: cover the classics well, add a few deep detours, and build in rest. Done right, an extended trip reveals a richer, more varied Japan than most visitors ever see.

title: 5 Days in Japan: A Short-Trip Itinerary
content:
Five days in Japan is short, but it's absolutely worthwhile — the key is to keep it tight and not try to see everything. With careful focus on Tokyo and Kyoto, you can still experience the country's two essential faces — modern neon energy and centuries-old tradition — without either one feeling rushed. Here's how to make every single day count, hour by hour if needed.

The strategy for a short trip

With only five days, don't spread yourself thin. Stick to two cities — Tokyo and Kyoto — connected by one Shinkansen ride, and accept that you'll skip some things (that's what a return trip is for). Prioritize the absolute highlights and group each day by area to avoid wasting time in transit — every hour spent crossing town to catch "one more thing" is an hour not spent actually experiencing wherever you already are, and on a trip this short that trade-off compounds fast.

Days 1–2: Tokyo

Day 1. Arrive, sort an IC card and data, drop bags. Spend the afternoon on the west side — Shibuya Crossing, Harajuku, and Meiji Shrine — keeping it light if you're jet-lagged. On a five-day trip you genuinely can't afford to lose day 2 to exhaustion, so err on the side of an early dinner and bed over squeezing in one more sight.

Day 2. Old Tokyo: Senso-ji in Asakusa, Tokyo Skytree for the view, and either Akihabara or teamLab depending on your interests. Cap it with an izakaya dinner. Skip Ginza and the further-out neighborhoods this trip — they're real Tokyo, but a five-day itinerary doesn't have room for a third Tokyo day.

Day 3: Travel to Kyoto + Fushimi Inari

Morning Shinkansen to Kyoto (about 2h15m). Drop your bags and head to Fushimi Inari in the afternoon to walk through the iconic red torii gate tunnels — magical in the late-afternoon light as crowds thin. You don't need to walk the entire mountain trail to the summit; the first 20-30 minutes through the densest cluster of torii gates covers the part almost everyone comes for, and turning back there rather than pushing on saves real energy for the days ahead.

Days 4–5: Kyoto

Day 4. Eastern Kyoto: the Higashiyama streets up to Kiyomizu-dera, then Gion at dusk with dinner on Pontocho Alley.

Day 5. Arashiyama's bamboo grove early, then Kinkaku-ji, before heading to the airport — ideally flying out of Kansai (KIX) to avoid returning to Tokyo. Build real buffer into this day: an afternoon flight gives you breathing room if the morning runs long, while an evening flight risks a stressful dash to the airport with your bags in tow.

What you're (deliberately) skipping

Five days means leaving out day trips like Hakone and Nara, plus Osaka — and that's fine. Trying to add them would turn a relaxed short trip into an exhausting dash. Save them for next time; almost everyone who visits Japan comes back. You're also skipping most of the "second-tier" Tokyo and Kyoto neighborhoods — Shinjuku's nightlife, Kyoto's Nishiki Market, a proper temple crawl beyond the two or three biggest names — which is a genuinely different experience from a 10-day trip, not just a shorter version of one.

Tips

  • Fly open-jaw (into Tokyo, out of Kansai) — essential on a short trip to avoid a wasted backtrack.
  • Skip the JR Pass — for a single Tokyo–Kyoto round trip (really a one-way here), individual tickets are cheaper.
  • Pack light so the one city change is quick and painless — a carry-on-only approach genuinely changes how manageable train travel feels.
  • Book any must-do timed experiences (like teamLab) in advance, since you have no slack to reschedule.
  • Confirm your Kyoto hotel is walkable to a train or bus stop — on a trip this compressed, you can't afford long transfers eating into your two Kyoto days.

Is five days actually enough?

Honestly: it's enough to fall in love with Japan, not enough to see it properly. The itinerary above works because it's ruthless about scope — two cities, no day trips, no detours — and that ruthlessness is the whole trick. If you find yourself wanting to add "just one more stop" while reading this, that instinct is exactly what turns a smooth five-day trip into a rushed one; deciding what a short trip can and can't hold is a big part of what Japan, Worked Out helps with, whether this is your only trip or the first of several.

Bottom line

Five days is enough for a genuine taste of Japan if you stay focused on Tokyo and Kyoto and don't overreach. You'll see the neon and the temples, ride the bullet train, and eat brilliantly — a short but complete first impression that leaves you wanting more — and for a lot of travelers, that's the whole point of a five-day trip in the first place.

title: Best Onsen Towns Near Tokyo and Kyoto
content:
You don't have to venture deep into the mountains to experience an onsen (hot spring) on a first trip. Several classic hot-spring areas sit within easy reach of Tokyo and the Kansai region, perfect for an overnight ryokan stay or even a day visit. Soaking in mineral-rich waters — ideally outdoors with a view — is one of Japan's quintessential pleasures, and you can fit it into almost any itinerary. Here are the most accessible options and how to choose.

Near Tokyo

Hakone

Hakone is the go-to hot-spring escape from Tokyo — close, scenic, and packed with onsen ryokan, with the bonus of Mt Fuji views on clear days and a fun loop of mountain railways, a ropeway over a steaming volcanic valley, and a boat across Lake Ashi. It's the easiest and most popular choice for combining hot springs with sightseeing, and works as an overnight or even a long day trip. The variety of baths — from grand ryokan to public bathhouses with valley views — makes it ideal for first-timers.

Other options reachable from Tokyo

Beyond Hakone, several hot-spring areas in the mountains north and west of Tokyo offer a more rustic, traditional atmosphere with fewer crowds. Places like Kusatsu (one of Japan's most famous hot-spring resorts, known for its dramatic central hot-water field) and the historic riverside town of Kinugawa near Nikko reward the slightly longer journey with classic onsen-town charm — wooden inns, steaming baths, and quiet streets. Nikko Yumoto, up in the highlands beyond the famous shrines, combines hot springs with mountain scenery. If you have time for an overnight and want something more off the beaten path than Hakone, these are worth considering.

Near Kyoto and Osaka

Kinosaki Onsen

From the Kansai region, Kinosaki Onsen is a beloved hot-spring town famous for its picturesque willow-lined canal and the tradition of strolling between its seven public bathhouses in your yukata and wooden sandals (geta), bath-hopping from one to the next — staying at a Kinosaki ryokan typically includes free access to all seven, which is most of the appeal of an overnight here over a day visit. It's a postcard-perfect onsen experience and one of the most atmospheric in the country. It's a popular overnight trip from Kyoto or Osaka, though it's a couple of hours away by train — best enjoyed as an overnight rather than a rushed day trip.

Closer soaks

There are also hot-spring options closer to Kyoto and Osaka for those short on time. Arima Onsen, tucked behind the mountains near Kobe, is one of Japan's oldest and most storied hot-spring towns and is reachable on a day trip from Osaka or Kyoto, known for its distinctive Kin-no-Yu ("gold," iron-rich reddish-brown) and Gin-no-Yu ("silver," carbonated) waters — the two public bathhouses sit within easy walking distance of each other, so trying both back to back is the classic Arima move. For a first trip focused on Kyoto, though, many travelers simply book a ryokan with its own onsen bath rather than traveling to a dedicated hot-spring town.

Day trip or overnight?

To truly enjoy an onsen town, an overnight stay in a ryokan is ideal — you get the evening and morning soaks, the multi-course kaiseki dinner, the chance to wander the town in your yukata, and the relaxed pace that makes these places special. But if time is tight, somewhere like Hakone or Arima can be done as a day trip with a public bath visit. Either way, build in enough time to actually slow down — rushing an onsen rather defeats the purpose. An onsen night also pairs naturally with a day trip you're already taking (Hakone with Mt Fuji sightseeing, for instance).

What to expect

Onsen towns typically center on hot-spring ryokan plus a handful of public bathhouses you can enter for a small fee. Many ryokan offer both large communal baths and, increasingly, private or in-room baths. Remember the basics of onsen etiquette — wash thoroughly before entering, bathe nude, keep your towel out of the water — and if you have tattoos, look for tattoo-friendly establishments or book a private bath, as some places still restrict visible ink.

Booking ahead

Onsen ryokan in popular towns fill quickly, especially on weekends, holidays, and in peak cherry-blossom and autumn seasons. If a hot-spring night is on your itinerary, reserve early and check what meals and baths are included (most rates include dinner and breakfast). Confirm current access details and travel times for your specific dates when you book, since some towns involve a transfer or local bus. A little planning secures one of the most relaxing and memorable nights of a Japan trip — and deciding whether that night comes from a dedicated onsen-town detour or a ryokan tacked onto a day trip you're already taking is exactly the kind of routing call Japan, Worked Out is built to help with.

title: Onsen Etiquette: How to Use a Japanese Hot Spring
content:
An onsen — a natural hot-spring bath — is one of Japan's great pleasures, but the etiquette can feel intimidating the first time, especially for Americans unused to communal bathing. The good news is that the rules are simple and logical once you know them, and following them shows respect and lets you relax. Here's exactly how it works, step by step.

The basics: wash before you soak

The single most important rule: you wash thoroughly before entering the bath. Onsen are for soaking in clean water, not for cleaning yourself. Inside the bathing area you'll find washing stations — usually a low stool, a handheld shower, a bucket, and provided soap and shampoo — where you sit, scrub down completely, and rinse off every trace of suds before getting into the communal bath. The shared water stays clean precisely because everyone washes first. This is the rule most worth getting right, and locals will notice if you skip it.

No swimsuits — bathing is nude

Traditional onsen are enjoyed nude; swimsuits are not worn in the baths. Baths are almost always gender-separated (look for the curtains — typically red/blue or the kanji for man and woman), so you'll be among others of the same gender, and it's completely normal and matter-of-fact — nobody is paying attention to you. If communal nude bathing isn't for you, look for ryokan or facilities with private baths (kashikiri) you can reserve, or rooms with their own in-room onsen bath.

The small towel

You'll typically be given or bring a small towel. Use it for a bit of modesty while walking around and for washing, but don't put it in the bath water — the custom is to fold it and rest it on your head, or set it on the rocks at the edge of the bath. Bring it back out with you to dry off in the changing area (there's usually a separate larger towel for drying back at your room or locker).

Step by step, your first time

  1. Remove your shoes/slippers before the changing room if you haven't already.
  2. In the changing room, undress completely and store everything in a basket or locker.
  3. Enter the bathing area with just your small towel.
  4. Sit at a washing station and clean yourself thoroughly — scrub, shampoo, rinse fully.
  5. Rinse the stool and area for the next person.
  6. Enter the bath slowly (the water is hot), keeping your towel out of the water.
  7. Soak, relax, and enjoy; step out to cool off if needed.
  8. When done, you can rinse off or — as many do — leave the mineral water on your skin.

Other key rules

  • Tie up long hair so it doesn't touch the water.
  • Don't swim, splash, or be loud — onsen are for quiet relaxation, not play.
  • Stay hydrated and don't overdo it — the hot water can be intense; step out and cool down if you feel lightheaded, and rest between soaks.
  • No phones or cameras in the bathing area, ever, for everyone's privacy.
  • Don't bring your own soap into the bath or wash in the soaking pool.
  • Re-enter the changing room reasonably dry so you don't soak the floor.

A note on tattoos

Some onsen restrict guests with visible tattoos, due to historical associations with organized crime. Policies vary widely, and many places — especially in tourist areas and newer facilities — are increasingly relaxed; some allow covering a small tattoo with a patch, and others offer private baths. Because this varies by establishment and continues to change, it's worth checking the specific onsen's current policy ahead of time if you have tattoos (we cover this in detail in our dedicated guide).

A health note worth taking seriously

Onsen water often runs hot (40°C/104°F or higher), and the combination of heat, mineral content, and a long soak is a real strain on the body — not just a comfort issue. If you have heart or blood pressure conditions, are pregnant, or have been drinking alcohol, check with staff or skip the hottest bath, keep soaks short, and never soak alone if you're at all unsure how your body will react. Dizziness on standing up (known locally as "the onsen effect") is common enough that most facilities post warnings about it — take it as a genuine caution, not overcaution.

Relax and enjoy

Once you've got the basics down — wash first, no swimsuit, towel out of the water, keep quiet — an onsen is pure bliss, especially an outdoor bath (rotenburo) in a scenic mountain or garden setting. Locals are forgiving of visitors making an honest effort, so don't be nervous about getting every detail perfect. It's a deeply relaxing, quintessentially Japanese experience, and one well worth seeking out at least once on your trip — enough so that choosing an onsen town as part of your route, rather than treating it as an afterthought, is worth real consideration, which is where Japan, Worked Out comes in.
excerpt: Japan's hot-spring baths have clear rules — wash first, no swimsuits, no towels in the water. Here's how to enjoy an onsen respectfully as a first-timer.

title: Tattoos and Onsen: What Travelers Need to Know
content:
If you have tattoos and want to experience a Japanese onsen, it's worth understanding the situation ahead of time. Tattoos can complicate hot-spring visits in Japan, but there are good, reliable workarounds, and attitudes are gradually shifting as the country welcomes more visitors from abroad. With a little planning, having ink doesn't have to mean missing out on one of the country's signature experiences — plenty of heavily tattooed travelers soak every trip without incident once they know the workarounds. Here's what to know.

Why tattoos are an issue

Historically, tattoos in Japan carried strong associations with organized crime (the yakuza), and as a result many onsen, public baths, swimming pools, and gyms adopted rules barring guests with visible tattoos. These rules were aimed at that historical association rather than at foreign tourists — but they often apply to everyone regardless, so a small, meaningful, or purely decorative tattoo that's completely unremarkable at home may still run into a posted no-tattoo policy at a Japanese bath. It's not personal; it's a blanket rule many establishments have long maintained, and staff enforcing it are simply following house policy, not making a judgment about you specifically.

The situation is changing

Attitudes are relaxing, especially as Japan welcomes more international visitors. Many establishments — particularly in tourist-heavy areas, newer facilities, and places used to foreign guests — are more flexible than they used to be, and some have dropped tattoo restrictions entirely. But there is no single national rule: policies vary enormously from one establishment to the next, and a place down the road may take the opposite stance. The only reliable approach is to check the specific establishment's current policy rather than assume.

Your options as a tattooed traveler

  • Book a private bath. Many ryokan offer private or family baths (kashikiri) you can reserve for a set time, or rooms with their own private onsen bath. This sidesteps the issue entirely and is by far the most reliable solution — and a lovely experience in its own right.
  • Cover small tattoos. For small tattoos, a waterproof cover patch or skin-tone bandage is sometimes accepted — but ask the establishment first, as this isn't universally allowed and won't work for large pieces.
  • Find tattoo-friendly onsen. A growing number of onsen explicitly welcome tattoos, and there are online guides and lists dedicated to finding them. It's worth seeking these out if you want the communal bathing experience.
  • Choose your destination accordingly. Some hot-spring towns and regions are known for being more tattoo-tolerant than others, so a little research before you pick where to go pays off.
  • Ask ahead. When booking a ryokan or planning an onsen visit, simply ask about their tattoo policy in advance so there are no surprises at the door.

What about covering up?

Cover patches work for small, isolated tattoos and are widely sold, but they're not a solution for sleeves, back pieces, or large designs. Don't rely on covering a large tattoo and hoping it goes unnoticed — if it's spotted, staff may politely but firmly ask you to leave the bathing area, which is an awkward situation for everyone and avoidable entirely with a little planning. When in doubt, the private-bath route avoids the problem completely.

Be respectful either way

If a place has a no-tattoo policy, respect it rather than trying to conceal a large tattoo and risk an uncomfortable confrontation. There are enough tattoo-friendly establishments and private-bath options that you don't need to push against the rules at a place that doesn't allow them. Approaching it with that mindset keeps the experience pleasant for you and for the establishment.

Where policies tend to be stricter or looser

As a rough pattern (never a guarantee): older, traditional public bathhouses and rural onsen towns with a mostly local clientele tend to enforce no-tattoo rules more strictly, while large resort hotels, big-city hot spring facilities, and properties that market heavily to international visitors are more often tattoo-friendly or offer private options by default. That's a generalization worth checking against the specific place, not a rule to plan around blindly — the only sure thing is asking directly.

Confirm before you go

Because tattoo policies differ by establishment and continue to evolve, treat any specific guidance as a starting point and confirm the current rules with your chosen onsen or ryokan when you book. A quick question ahead of time — "do you allow guests with tattoos, or offer a private bath?" — saves disappointment at the door and lets you plan with confidence. With that bit of homework, tattooed travelers can absolutely enjoy Japan's wonderful hot springs — and if a private bath is your plan either way, it's worth choosing your one ryokan night with that requirement in mind from the start, which Japan, Worked Out can help factor in.

title: What Is a Ryokan? A First-Timer's Guide to Japanese Inns
content:
A ryokan is a traditional Japanese inn, and staying in one is one of the most memorable things you can do on a trip to Japan. It's less a hotel than a cultural experience — a window into traditional hospitality (omotenashi), aesthetics, and rhythm. For many first-timers, a night in a ryokan becomes a highlight of the entire trip. Here's what to expect and how to enjoy your stay.

What a ryokan is

Ryokan date back centuries, some over a thousand years, and center on traditional Japanese hospitality and design. Rooms typically feature tatami-mat floors, sliding paper screens (shoji), low furniture, a small sitting area, and futon bedding laid out directly on the floor — often set up by staff in the evening while you're at dinner and put away in the morning. Many ryokan have hot-spring baths (especially in onsen towns), and meals are usually a central part of the experience. They range from simple, affordable family-run inns to opulent luxury retreats costing as much as a fine hotel.

What's usually included

Most ryokan stays include dinner and breakfast, and the dinner is often a multi-course kaiseki meal — an artful, seasonal procession of small, beautifully presented local dishes that's a culinary experience in itself. This is a big part of what you're paying for, and a major reason ryokan cost more than a basic hotel: you're paying for the meals, the service, and the experience, not just the room. Breakfast is typically a traditional Japanese spread (grilled fish, rice, miso soup, pickles), though some offer a Western option. Always check whether meals are included when you book, as it dramatically changes the value comparison.

The typical flow of a stay

A ryokan stay has a gentle, customary rhythm:

  • Arrival: you remove your shoes at the entrance (genkan) and change into provided slippers; staff often greet you warmly and may serve welcome tea and a sweet in your room.
  • Yukata: you'll be given a yukata (a casual cotton robe) to wear around the inn — and, at onsen ryokan, to and from the baths. It's perfectly acceptable to wear it to dinner and around the grounds.
  • Bath: many guests bathe before dinner; if there's an onsen, follow the usual etiquette (wash before entering, no swimsuit).
  • Dinner: often served at a set time, either in your room or a dining area — a leisurely kaiseki feast.
  • Futon: while you dine, staff typically lay out your futon bedding on the tatami.
  • Breakfast: a traditional morning meal, often at a set time, followed by checkout.

Etiquette basics

  • Take your shoes off where indicated and use the slippers provided — with separate toilet slippers where present (don't wear those out of the bathroom).
  • Step on tatami in socks or bare feet, not slippers.
  • Wear the yukata with the left side wrapped over the right (right-over-left is used only for dressing the deceased, so this detail matters).
  • Be quiet and respectful — ryokan are tranquil places valued for their calm.
  • If there's a shared bath, follow onsen etiquette: wash thoroughly before entering, no swimsuit, towel out of the water.
  • There's no tipping.

Who should stay in one

A ryokan suits any traveler curious about traditional Japan, and it's especially magical in an onsen town (where you can soak in hot springs) or in Kyoto (where the traditional setting matches the culture). Even a single night adds a memorable dimension to a trip otherwise spent in city hotels. The trade-offs to be aware of: less privacy and flexibility than a Western hotel, set meal and bath times, and the floor-futon sleeping style, which isn't for everyone. But most first-timers find it a genuine highlight rather than a hardship.

Private baths and rooms with their own onsen

If the idea of a shared communal bath gives you pause — because of modesty, tattoos, or simply preference — look for a ryokan offering a private bath (kashikiri-buro), bookable for your room for a set window, or a room with its own attached open-air bath (rotenburo-tsuki). These cost more but sidestep the shared-bath question entirely, and they're increasingly common even in mid-range properties as demand from foreign travelers has grown.

Booking

Ryokan — especially the well-regarded ones in popular onsen towns and in Kyoto — book up early in peak seasons, so reserve ahead. Check exactly what's included (meals, private vs shared bath, room type), and note any set dinner times. International booking sites list many ryokan now, though some of the best small, family-run properties still only take reservations through Japanese-language sites or by phone — a hotel booking service or your accommodation's concierge can sometimes bridge that gap. Prices vary enormously, from budget family inns to luxury escapes, so there's a ryokan for most budgets. It's well worth the planning for an experience you simply can't get anywhere else — a night of traditional hospitality that lingers in the memory long after the trip.

Fitting a ryokan night into your route

The honest complication: a ryokan stay works best when you're not also trying to pack in a full day of sightseeing, since the whole point is slowing down for the bath-dinner-futon rhythm. That makes WHERE you put your one ryokan night — a Hakone day trip extended overnight, a Kyoto splurge, an onsen town detour — a real trade-off against the rest of a tight itinerary, not a free add-on. Japan, Worked Out works through exactly where a ryokan night earns its place.

title: Green Car or Ordinary: Is the Japan Rail Pass Upgrade Worth It?
content:
Every Japan Rail Pass comes in two tiers, and the more expensive one is presented as the comfortable choice without anyone explaining what it costs per journey. The upgrade is real and so is the premium. This guide covers what the Green Car tier costs, what you get for it, the arithmetic that decides it, and the specific travellers for whom it is worth paying.

What the upgrade actually costs

The seven-day Green Car pass costs ¥70,000 against ¥50,000 for the ordinary tier — a premium of ¥20,000 for the week. That is the whole decision in one line, and it is a larger gap than most travellers expect, because the two tiers are usually presented side by side as though the difference were marginal.

The premium across the longer passes

The gap widens with duration rather than staying proportional in absolute terms. The fourteen-day pass runs ¥110,000 in Green against ¥80,000 ordinary, a ¥30,000 premium, and the twenty-one-day version stretches it to ¥40,000. A longer trip does not make the upgrade proportionally cheaper — it makes the cash difference bigger.

Children aged six to eleven pay half on both tiers, so a family upgrading everybody multiplies the premium rather than absorbing it.

What the money buys

A Green Car seat is laid out two-and-two across the carriage instead of the ordinary car's two-and-three, which is the single most noticeable difference. Seats are wider, recline further, and carry a proper footrest. Carriages are quieter because they are rarely full, and an attendant works the car with a trolley rather than the ordinary car's occasional pass-through.

What it does not buy

The upgrade does not make you faster. Green Car carriages ride the same trains on the same timetable, and the fastest Nozomi and Mizuho services remain outside what the national pass covers at either tier — the upgrade does not unlock them. There is no lounge access, no included food, and no priority boarding. You are buying space and quiet, nothing else.

The arithmetic per journey

Divide the ¥20,000 premium by the number of long journeys your route actually contains, and the upgrade resolves into a per-leg price. A typical first trip makes two long journeys, which prices the upgrade at ¥10,000 per leg — more than most travellers would pay for a seat upgrade if it were presented that way at the counter. Four legs brings it to ¥5,000 each.

Comparing it to the journey itself

Set that against the fare for the journey. A reserved ordinary seat from Tokyo to Kyoto costs about ¥13,850, so a ¥10,000 per-leg upgrade is close to paying a second time for the same trip. At ¥5,000 a leg the ratio starts to look like an ordinary premium-cabin decision rather than an extravagance.

The honest reading is that the upgrade gets cheaper the more you travel, which is the same condition that makes the pass itself pay. If your route is too short to justify the ordinary pass, it is much too short to justify the Green one.

Every Green seat is reserved

There is no non-reserved Green Car, which is a structural difference rather than a comfort one. Every seat in the carriage is booked, so the tier removes the possibility of standing or hunting for a free seat on a busy departure — the failure mode that makes ordinary-car travel unpleasant in the peak weeks. You still have to make the reservation; the pass covers it at no extra charge.

What that is worth in practice

On a quiet Tuesday it is worth nothing, because the ordinary reserved car is equally guaranteed and equally empty. On the heaviest travel days of the year it is worth a great deal, because Green Cars are the last carriages to fill and often the only ones with availability when a reservation is made late.

When the premium is easiest to justify

Three situations make the Green Car worth its ¥20,000. Long single legs — anything beyond the Tokyo to Kyoto distance, where you are seated for three hours or more — convert space into genuine rest. Travelling in the busiest weeks, when ordinary reserved seats book out and the non-reserved cars fill, buys availability rather than comfort. And travelling with large luggage is simply easier in a carriage with room.

A worked comparison

Take two routes. A first trip flying into Tokyo, crossing to Kyoto and flying home makes two long legs, so the premium prices at ¥10,000 each and the ordinary car is plainly the right answer. A two-week route that adds Hiroshima, returns north through the mountains and uses fast trains for several longer excursions might make six, which brings the premium to a little over ¥3,300 a journey — roughly a quarter of the fare, and a defensible upgrade on legs you are seated for hours.

The traveller it suits

Height is the underrated factor. The ordinary car is comfortable for most people and tight for anyone over about six feet, particularly on a three-hour leg with a case underfoot. If that describes you, the upgrade stops being a luxury and becomes the difference between arriving rested and arriving stiff.

Age and mobility matter for the same reason. A wider seat that reclines properly, in a quiet carriage with an attendant who comes to you, is worth more to some travellers than to others, and that is a personal calculation rather than an arithmetic one.

Who should not take it

Most first trips should stay in the ordinary car. The classic route makes two long journeys, prices the upgrade at ¥10,000 each, and spends that money on a seat that is already perfectly comfortable for the distance involved. Japanese ordinary-car standards are high — clean, quiet, reliably punctual, with more legroom than an American domestic flight in economy.

The upgrade is a genuine improvement on an already good product, which is exactly the kind of purchase that is easy to talk yourself into and hard to feel afterwards. Buy it because your route is long or your frame is tall, not because the tier exists.

The channel detail that changes the price

From 1 October 2026 the overseas-agency price for the seven-day Green pass rises to ¥74,000, while buying online through the official reservation site is unaffected. The ordinary tier moves the same way, to ¥53,000 through an agency.

That reverses a piece of standing advice. Going through an agent used to be the convenient route and is now simply the more expensive one, and the gap applies to whichever tier you choose.

Making the call

Price the upgrade per leg before you price it per week, because ¥20,000 sounds like a fee and ¥10,000 a journey sounds like what it is. Count your long journeys, divide, and decide against that number rather than against the headline.

Which tier to buy sits downstream of how much long-distance travel your route contains in the first place, and working that out in the right order is what Japan, Worked Out is built to do.

title: How to Ride the Shinkansen (Bullet Train)
content:
Riding the Shinkansen — Japan's famous bullet train — is one of the great pleasures of a trip: fast, smooth, punctual, and remarkably comfortable. It's also far easier to use than first-timers expect once you know the basics. Here's a complete first-timer's guide, from buying your ticket to enjoying an ekiben cruising along at close to 200 mph.

Why the Shinkansen is special

The Shinkansen whisks you between cities at high speed, city center to city center, with none of the airport-style hassle of security lines and distant terminals. The classic Tokyo–Kyoto run takes only about two and a quarter hours and is punctual almost to the second — the Tokaido line's average delay has run well under a minute for two decades running, a level of reliability that would be unthinkable for a US train (or, often, a US flight). Beyond being superb transport, the ride itself is a bucket-list experience: gliding past countryside, rice paddies, and, on clear days, a glimpse of Mt Fuji from the window (sit on the right-hand side heading from Tokyo toward Kyoto/Osaka for the best chance).

Buying tickets

  • With a Japan Rail Pass: the pass covers most Shinkansen (with exceptions for the very fastest Nozomi/Mizuho services, which need a supplement) — reserve seats for free at JR ticket offices or machines, or simply ride the non-reserved cars.
  • Without a pass: buy a ticket at JR ticket machines (English menus available) or ticket offices for your route. You'll typically get a base fare ticket plus a limited-express (Shinkansen) ticket — feed both through the gate together.
  • Reserved vs non-reserved: a reserved seat (shitei-seki) guarantees you a spot and is worth it in busy periods and holidays; non-reserved cars (jiyu-seki) are first-come and cheaper, fine off-peak. You can also book some routes online in advance.

At the station

  • Look for the dedicated Shinkansen gates and platforms — they're separate from regular train gates and clearly signed in English.
  • Insert your ticket(s) into the gate together (with a pass, use the staffed gate or tap as directed).
  • Platform displays show your train, its exact departure time, and where each car stops — line up at your car number marked on the platform floor.
  • Trains stop only briefly, so be ready to board promptly at your marked spot.

Finding and using your seat

  • Cars are numbered; a reserved ticket shows your car and seat number.
  • Non-reserved seating is in specific cars (shown on signage, often cars 1–3) — board those and take any free seat.
  • There's generous legroom, fold-down trays, power outlets at most seats, and overhead racks for smaller bags.
  • Seats can often be rotated to face your group — there's a foot pedal or lever, or staff will help.

Luggage: the oversized-baggage rule

One rule worth knowing in advance: on the Tokaido, Sanyo, and Kyushu Shinkansen lines (the main routes including Tokyo–Kyoto–Osaka–Hiroshima–Fukuoka), large luggage with total dimensions over 160 cm (length + width + height) requires a free reservation for an "oversized baggage" seat — a regular reserved seat with dedicated space behind it. Reserving it costs nothing, but boarding with such a bag without the reservation can incur a fee. Most normal suitcases are fine in the overhead racks or the space behind the last row; this rule targets the biggest bags. If you're traveling with large luggage, just request the oversized-baggage seat when you reserve.

Onboard etiquette and tips

  • Keep quiet — conversations are low, phones on silent, and calls taken standing in the vestibules between cars, not at your seat.
  • It's customary and delightful to enjoy an ekiben (a station bento box) on board — buy one at the station beforehand along with a drink; it's part of the experience.
  • Recline considerately (a glance back is polite) and keep aisles clear.
  • Trains depart exactly on time — be on the platform a few minutes early.
  • There are restrooms, and on some trains a trolley service or vending.

Practical notes

  • Arrive with a few minutes to spare to find your car's queue spot on the platform.
  • The fastest Nozomi and Mizuho services aren't covered by the standard nationwide JR Pass without paying a supplement — the slightly slower Hikari and Sakura are covered and only a few minutes longer on most routes.
  • Keep all ticket pieces until you've exited the gate at your destination.
  • Reserve the oversized-baggage spot in advance if you're carrying a large suitcase.

Bottom line

The Shinkansen is fast, effortless, and a genuine joy to ride. Buy your ticket (or use your pass), find the Shinkansen platform, line up at your car number, grab an ekiben, mind the luggage rule if your bag is large, and settle in for one of the smoothest, most iconic train journeys in the world — and once you've ridden it once, deciding how many more times to ride it (versus flying or bussing between cities) becomes part of the bigger route-planning picture that Japan, Worked Out works through in detail.

title: Is the Japan Rail Pass Worth It?
content:
The Japan Rail Pass is one of the first things travelers research — and one of the most misunderstood, especially since a major price increase changed the math. It can still be excellent value or a clear waste of money depending entirely on your itinerary. Here's how to decide for your trip, with the current pricing reality.

What the Japan Rail Pass is

The Japan Rail Pass (JR Pass) is a special ticket, available to foreign tourists, that gives unlimited travel on most JR trains — including many Shinkansen bullet trains — for a set number of consecutive days (7, 14, or 21). It's sold in nationwide and various regional versions. The idea is simple: one upfront price for unlimited JR travel during the validity window.

The price reality (and why the math changed)

In late 2023 the nationwide pass rose sharply in price — by roughly 65–70% — which fundamentally changed when it's worth buying. As of 2026 the nationwide Ordinary pass costs roughly ¥50,000 for 7 days, ¥80,000 for 14 days, and ¥100,000 for 21 days (the Green Car version costs more; children 6–11 are half price). Note that prices purchased through overseas channels are set to rise again on October 1, 2026 (the 7-day Ordinary pass to about ¥53,000), so check the current figure for your travel dates.

When it's worth it

The pass pays off when you do a lot of long-distance JR travel within the validity window — more than it used to take. The key shift to understand: a single round trip between Tokyo and Kyoto on the Shinkansen now runs roughly ¥28,000, which only covers a bit more than half the ¥50,000 seven-day pass. So that classic round trip alone no longer justifies the pass. You need substantial additional long-distance travel on top — for example adding Hiroshima, Fukuoka, or several more intercity Shinkansen hops within the seven days — to push past the break-even point. For trips with that much rail movement, the pass is convenient and can save money.

When it's NOT worth it

After the price rise, the pass is not worth it for many common first-trip itineraries:

  • You're staying mostly in one city (e.g. just Tokyo), where local transit isn't the pass's strength and individual fares are cheap.
  • You're doing the classic Tokyo + Kyoto trip with just one round trip between them — individual Shinkansen tickets will almost certainly cost less than a full nationwide pass.
  • Your long-distance travel is spread out beyond the consecutive-day window, so you'd waste paid days.

For a lot of first-timers doing Tokyo plus Kyoto, the honest answer now is: skip the nationwide pass and buy individual tickets, unless you're adding significant extra distance.

How to decide: do the math

The reliable method hasn't changed, even if the answer often has: add up the individual fares for the long-distance JR trips you actually plan to take, then compare that total to the current price of the pass for the matching number of days. If your fares clearly exceed the pass price, buy the pass; if they don't, buy tickets as you go. Because both the pass price and individual fares change over time, always check current prices for your specific route before committing.

Important notes

  • The pass covers JR lines — not private railways or city subways (your IC card handles those).
  • It does not cover the fastest Nozomi and Mizuho Shinkansen without paying a supplement; use the covered Hikari and Sakura services, which are only marginally slower on most routes.
  • Regional JR passes (e.g. Kansai-area or wider west-Japan passes) can be far better value if your travel is concentrated in one region — often worth more consideration now than the pricey nationwide pass.
  • Buy and activate per the current official process; eligibility is for short-term foreign visitors (Temporary Visitor status).

The pass decision is really a route decision

Notice that the pass math depends entirely on something you haven't necessarily decided yet: how many cities you're visiting and how far apart they are. That's not a coincidence — the JR Pass question and the "how many bases, in what order" question are really the same decision looked at from two angles. Settle your route first, with real distances and a real day count, and the pass math falls out of it almost automatically; try to answer the pass question in isolation and you're guessing. Japan, Worked Out works through routing and rail costs together for exactly this reason.

Bottom line

Since the big price hike, the nationwide Japan Rail Pass is worth it only for itineraries with a lot of long-distance JR travel — not for single-city trips or a simple Tokyo–Kyoto round trip, where it no longer pays for itself. Don't buy it by default. Add up your planned fares, compare to the current pass price, look at regional passes as an alternative, and let the math decide for your specific route.
excerpt: The Japan Rail Pass offers unlimited JR travel, but it's not always the best deal. Here's how to decide whether it's worth it for your trip.

title: What a Japan Rail Route Actually Costs Without a Pass
content:
Deciding whether a rail pass is worth buying requires knowing what the same journeys cost without one, and that number is surprisingly hard to find stated plainly. This guide prices the legs a first trip actually makes, explains how a Japanese fare is built, and gives you a method for costing your own route in about ten minutes.

What the main journeys cost

A reserved ordinary-car seat from Tokyo to Kyoto costs about ¥13,850 one way on a Hikari service. Tokyo to Shin-Osaka is slightly more. Travelling without a seat reservation is a few hundred yen cheaper, and the fastest Nozomi services cost a few hundred more than the Hikari.

How a Japanese fare is built

A Shinkansen ticket is not one price but two added together: a base fare for the distance, and a limited-express surcharge for the speed. That is why the numbers look oddly specific, and why a seat reservation is a separate small charge on top rather than part of the ticket.

The practical consequence is that comparing headline prices between routes can mislead. A journey twice as far is not twice the price, because the base fare scales with distance while the surcharge does not scale the same way.

Costing your own route

Pricing a Japanese rail route is straightforward once you stop thinking in days and start thinking in legs. Write down every long journey your itinerary makes — city to city, plus any day trip that uses a fast train — and price each one at roughly the Tokyo–Kyoto figure per comparable distance. The total is what your trip costs without any pass.

The legs a typical first trip makes

Most first itineraries contain two long journeys: into the country at one city, across to the second, and home. Some add a third if they reach further west or return by a different route. Very few first trips exceed four, which is the number that matters when any pass is being considered.

Short day trips from Tokyo or Kyoto usually run on local and rapid services at a fraction of bullet-train prices, so they rarely change the arithmetic much. It is the long inter-city legs that carry the cost.

Three worked routes

Pricing three common shapes makes the method concrete. A classic first week — into Tokyo, across to Kyoto, home from Osaka — contains one long leg and costs about one Tokyo–Kyoto fare in total. Ten days adding Hiroshima contains three long legs. A two-week loop that returns north from Kansai and reaches Kanazawa or Takayama contains four or five.

Those totals are the whole comparison. The first route cannot justify a national pass at any price; the third is exactly the shape where one starts to pay. Nothing about the decision requires more analysis than counting.

Day trips barely move the number

Day trips from Tokyo to Kamakura or Nikko, or from Kyoto to Nara, run largely on local and rapid services at a fraction of bullet-train prices. They matter to the day's plan and hardly at all to the ticketing arithmetic, which is worth knowing before you build an itinerary around extracting value from unlimited travel.

Reserved or not

Reserving a seat on a Japanese bullet train costs a few hundred yen and is worth it on almost every occasion a first-time visitor travels. Non-reserved cars exist on most services and are genuinely usable outside peak periods, but they fill on holiday weekends and at the start and end of major travel periods, which is precisely when an American visitor is most likely to be moving with luggage.

Travelling with large suitcases adds a wrinkle: oversized baggage on the busiest lines requires a reserved space, booked with the seat. It costs nothing extra if you do it at the time of booking and is awkward to fix afterwards.

When the point-to-point approach wins

Paying per journey wins whenever the route is short on long legs, which describes most first trips. It also wins on flexibility, because you are not trying to compress your travel into a fixed window to extract value from something already paid for — a distortion that quietly shapes a lot of Japan itineraries.

Buying tickets is straightforward. Machines at every major station carry English interfaces, staffed ticket offices handle anything unusual, and reservations can be made from a few weeks ahead down to minutes before departure if seats remain.

Comparing honestly

Once you have your route total, the comparison to any pass is a single subtraction. If your legs come to less than the pass price, the pass is a loss no matter how attractive the unlimited travel sounds; if they exceed it, the pass wins and the margin tells you by how much. The pass side of that comparison covers what the national pass includes.

Doing the sum in the other order — buying first, planning after — is the mistake that costs most. Routing and ticketing are one decision, and Japan, Worked Out treats them that way.

title: Regional JR Passes vs the National Japan Rail Pass
content:
The Japan Rail Pass used to be the automatic first purchase of any Japan trip. Since the price rise it no longer is, and a great deal of advice online has not caught up. This guide covers what the national pass costs now, the arithmetic that decides whether it pays, how the regional passes compare, and a channel change arriving on 1 October 2026 that reverses some standing advice.

What the national pass costs

The national Japan Rail Pass costs ¥50,000 for seven days in the ordinary car, with fourteen- and twenty-one-day versions and a Green car tier above it. Children aged six to eleven pay half. That seven-day figure is the one every calculation below turns on.

Why the advice online is stale

In October 2023 the seven-day ordinary pass rose from about ¥29,650 to its current price — an increase of roughly sixty-five to seventy per cent in a single step. A great deal of the English-language guidance that recommends buying the pass reflexively was written before that, and has never been revised. The pass did not merely get more expensive; it stopped being the default answer.

The arithmetic that actually decides it

A reserved seat from Tokyo to Kyoto on a Hikari service — the fastest train the national pass covers — costs about ¥13,850 one way. Divide the pass price by that and the pass needs roughly four long journeys of similar distance before it pays for itself, which is about two round trips inside the seven-day window.

What that means for a normal first trip

The classic first trip flies into Tokyo, spends several days there, takes the bullet train to Kyoto, spends several more, and flies home. That is two long journeys, not four. On its own it does not come close to justifying the national pass, and buying one out of habit is a straightforward loss.

The picture changes if you add distance. A trip that also reaches Hiroshima, or that returns north from the Kansai region, or that uses the fast trains for several day trips, starts to accumulate the legs the pass needs. The honest test is to count your actual long journeys before you buy, not after.

Two details sit on the credit side of the ledger. The pass also covers local JR lines in the cities and the airport express from Narita, which is real value it is easy to forget. And it covers unlimited travel, so a spontaneous extra journey costs nothing once you hold one.

The fastest trains are not included

Nozomi and Mizuho services, the quickest on the Tokaido and Sanyo lines, are not covered by the national pass. Pass holders may ride them by buying a separate supplement, reported at around ¥4,960 for Tokyo to Kyoto. The Hikari, Sakura and Kodama services on the same tracks are fully covered and take roughly twenty minutes longer.

For most itineraries that twenty minutes is not worth paying for, but it matters if you are timing a connection or travelling at the end of a long day.

The regional passes

Regional passes cover one area of Japan rather than the whole country and cost a fraction of the national pass's price, which makes them the better fit for most first trips. The four that matter on a Tokyo–Kyoto–Osaka route are the JR East Tokyo Wide Pass for three days around Tokyo, the JR West Kansai Area Pass for one to four days around Osaka and Kyoto, the Kansai-Hiroshima Area Pass for five days if you are going west, and the JR Central Takayama-Hokuriku pass for the mountain route.

Reading them properly

The trap in the regional passes is coverage rather than price. The Kansai Area Pass, for example, covers local and rapid services but not the bullet train, which surprises people who assume any pass includes it. Check what each one excludes before buying — that is where the disappointment lives, not in the cost.

Regional passes also stack in a way the national pass does not. A three-day pass around Tokyo and a separate one around Kansai can cost far less than a week of national coverage while matching what you actually do.

Where you can buy, and a date to watch

The national pass is bought online through the official reservation site or as an Exchange Order from a designated travel agency abroad. In-person purchase at stations inside Japan ended on 1 October 2023 — you can still exchange a voucher at a station, which is not the same thing and is the distinction that strands people who plan to buy on arrival.

The 1 October 2026 change

From 1 October 2026 the overseas-agency price rises to ¥53,000 for the seven-day ordinary pass, with the longer durations and the Green tier rising in proportion. Buying online through the official site is not affected.

That inverts a piece of advice that has been repeated for years. Going through an agent used to be the convenient and sometimes cheaper route; from that date it is simply the more expensive one.

What the pass decision is really attached to

Notice what the arithmetic above actually depended on. Whether the pass pays is not a fact about the pass — it is a fact about how many long journeys your route contains, which depends on how many places you base yourself in, which depends on how long you have and what time of year you are coming. The pass question cannot be answered before the route question, and it is almost always asked first.

That is why so many first trips buy the wrong thing: the purchase gets made early, from habit, and the route that would have justified it is designed afterwards. Working out the route and the passes as one problem rather than two is what Japan, Worked Out is built to do.
excerpt: Since the 2023 price rise the national pass rarely pays for itself on a first trip. How the regional passes compare, and how to tell which — if either — is worth buying.

title: Kansai Airport to Kyoto and Osaka: Transfer Guide
content:
Kansai International Airport (KIX) is the main international gateway for the Kyoto/Osaka side of Japan — built on an artificial island in Osaka Bay — and a natural arrival or departure point for trips centered on western Japan. Getting from KIX into Kyoto or Osaka is straightforward by train, and well signed in English. Here's how to do it.

First steps on arrival

Before leaving the airport, set yourself up so the journey in is painless: grab an IC card (Suica, Pasmo, or the Kansai-region ICOCA — all interchangeable for most travel), and sort out mobile data (activate an eSIM, or pick up a SIM or pocket WiFi). Then head to the rail platforms, which are clearly signed and easy to find from the arrivals area. With a tap card and data in hand, you're ready to go.

From KIX to Kyoto

The most convenient option to Kyoto is the direct Haruka limited express, a JR airport train that runs from the airport straight to Kyoto Station in roughly 75–90 minutes. It's comfortable, with luggage space, and drops you at Kyoto's central transport hub, from which you can reach your accommodation by subway, bus, or taxi. A Japan Rail Pass or a regional pass (such as a Kansai-area pass) can cover the Haruka if you hold one; otherwise buy a ticket at the station — there are sometimes discounted package deals combining the Haruka with an ICOCA card for tourists, sold specifically to foreign passport holders at the airport counter — worth asking about even if you weren't planning to buy one there.

From KIX to Osaka

To central Osaka, you have a few main choices depending on your exact destination:

  • JR rapid trains connecting to central Osaka stations (like Tennoji and Osaka/Umeda), a budget-friendly option taking around an hour.
  • The Haruka limited express, which also serves the Osaka area (Tennoji, Shin-Osaka) en route to Kyoto — faster but pricier.
  • The Nankai railway (a private line), including its rapit limited express, which runs efficiently to Namba in southern Osaka — ideal if you're staying in the Minami/Namba area.

Travel time varies with your exact destination within the city, generally in the 45–70 minute range.

Other options

  • Limousine buses: direct airport buses run to major hotels and stations in Osaka, Kyoto, Kobe, and beyond — convenient if you have heavy luggage and your stop is covered, with no transfers.
  • Taxi: available but very expensive given the distance from the island; generally not recommended unless money is no object or you're a group with lots of bags splitting the fare.
  • Kobe: if your trip includes Kobe rather than Kyoto or Osaka, a direct limousine bus and the Kobe-Kansai Airport Bay Shuttle boat both connect KIX to the city, and are often faster than routing through Osaka first.

If you're picking up a Japan Rail Pass

Travelers exchanging a JR Pass voucher for the physical pass can do so right at the KIX JR ticket office on arrival, which saves a stop later — worth doing immediately if your itinerary starts with a JR-covered journey. If you're buying a regional ICOCA & Haruka discount ticket instead, the same ticket counters sell it, and it's usually cheaper than buying the IC card and Haruka fare separately.

Which to choose

  • Going to Kyoto: the direct Haruka limited express to Kyoto Station is the simplest, most comfortable choice.
  • Going to central/northern Osaka: JR rapid trains for value, or Haruka for speed to Shin-Osaka/Tennoji.
  • Going to Namba/southern Osaka: the Nankai line is the most direct.
  • Heavy luggage and a covered hotel: a limousine bus saves you transfers.
  • Have a JR Pass: use it on covered JR services like the Haruka and rapid trains.

Practical tips

  • Confirm current schedules and exact travel times for your specific destination and the time of day.
  • Buy tickets at clearly marked airport station counters and machines (English available), and look for tourist discount tickets.
  • Allow buffer time, especially on departure, for the journey back out to the island airport.
  • Consider an open-jaw flight (into Tokyo, out of KIX, or vice versa) to avoid backtracking on a Tokyo–Kyoto trip — it can save a lot of time, and it's one piece of a bigger route-planning decision that Japan, Worked Out covers in full.
  • The Haruka and other limited expresses need a separate ticket beyond your IC card (the card alone doesn't cover them).

Bottom line

From Kansai Airport, the direct Haruka train makes Kyoto easy (~75–90 min), while Osaka is reachable by JR rapid trains, the Haruka, the Nankai line, or a limousine bus in roughly an hour. Get your IC card and data sorted first, pick the train that fits your exact destination, and you'll be settled in western Japan in no time.

title: Getting from the Airport to Central Tokyo (Narita & Haneda)
content:
Tokyo has two airports, and which one you land at makes a real difference to your first hour in Japan. The good news: both are well connected, spotlessly run, and easy to navigate with clear English signage — so getting into the center is straightforward even when you're jet-lagged and hauling luggage. Here's how to do it from each.

First, know your airport

Tokyo's two gateways are Haneda (HND) and Narita (NRT). The key difference for arriving travelers: Haneda is much closer to central Tokyo, while Narita sits well outside the city in neighboring Chiba. If you had a choice when booking your flight, Haneda usually means a shorter, cheaper, quicker transfer into the city center. Either way, both airports are well connected by multiple rail and bus options, so you'll get into the city smoothly regardless of where you land.

Set yourself up before you leave the airport

Two quick things to do on arrival, before you head into the city, make everything easier:

  • Pick up a Suica or Pasmo IC card at a station ticket machine (English option available) — you'll tap it for every train, subway, bus, and many shops.
  • Sort mobile data — activate an eSIM, or grab a SIM card or pocket WiFi at an airport counter — so you have maps and translation from the moment you arrive.

With a tap card and data, the transfer (and the whole trip) becomes far less stressful.

From Haneda to central Tokyo

Haneda is the easy one — it's close, so the transfer is quick, roughly 30 minutes to central areas. Two main rail options carry you in:

  • Tokyo Monorail — connects to the JR Yamanote loop line at Hamamatsucho, useful for reaching stations around the loop.
  • Keikyu Line — links directly toward Shinagawa and onward into the network, convenient for many central hotels.

Both are affordable and fast, and your IC card works on them. A taxi or rideshare is an option that's merely pricey (not astronomical) from Haneda — worth it if you're exhausted, traveling with young kids, or in a group with lots of bags splitting the fare.

From Narita to central Tokyo

Narita is farther out, so plan on roughly 60 to 90 minutes into the center. The two standout train options:

  • Narita Express (N'EX) — a comfortable JR limited-express train running directly to major hubs like Tokyo, Shinjuku, and Shibuya stations. The simplest choice if your hotel is near one of those.
  • Keisei Skyliner — a fast train to Ueno and Nippori in the city's east, great if you're staying around Asakusa or that side of town.

There are also cheaper but slower local trains, and limousine buses that go directly to many hotels — handy if you have heavy luggage and want zero transfers. Avoid a straight taxi from Narita unless money is no object; the distance makes it extremely expensive.

Which to use

From Haneda, take the monorail or Keikyu and you'll be at your hotel fast. From Narita, match the train to your neighborhood — the N'EX for the Tokyo/Shinjuku/Shibuya side, the Skyliner for the Ueno/Asakusa side, or a limousine bus if your hotel is a direct stop and you're laden with bags. Note that these airport express trains need their own ticket (your IC card alone doesn't cover the N'EX or Skyliner). Get your IC card first, follow the clear English signs, and the rest is just tapping in. Which airport you land at is really the first move in a bigger question — how many cities you'll base in and in what order — and Japan, Worked Out walks through that sequencing in full.

Sending your luggage ahead (takkyubin)

One option most first-timers don't know about: Japan's takkyubin courier services (Yamato's Airport TA-Q-BIN is the biggest) will pick up your bags at the airport and deliver them to your hotel — same-day is possible from Haneda if you're at the counter by 11am, otherwise plan on next-day delivery, and it's hotel-only (not vacation rentals) — for a flat fee plus a small counter charge per bag. It's genuinely useful if you're heading straight to sightseeing rather than your hotel, or if you don't want to haul suitcases through a crowded train. Counters are at both Haneda and Narita arrivals; you'll need your hotel's address, which is worth having saved on your phone before you land.

Bottom line

Whichever airport you land at, getting into Tokyo is easy: sort an IC card and data on arrival, then take the train that matches your hotel's location. From Haneda you'll be in the center in about half an hour; from Narita, plan for an hour or more via the N'EX, Skyliner, or bus. With the airport transfer sorted, you're ready to dive into the city.

title: IC Card, Day Pass or Single Ticket: What to Use
content:
Japanese city transit offers three ways to pay, and most visitors default to whichever one they read about first. The difference over a week is modest in money and significant in friction. This guide covers what each costs, the coverage trap that catches people in Tokyo, and the simple test for which one your day needs.

The default answer is the IC card

For most first-time visitors in Tokyo or Kyoto, a stored-value IC card — Suica, Pasmo or Icoca — is the right default. Individual subway rides run roughly ¥180 to ¥330 depending on distance, a typical sightseeing day involves three or four of them, and tapping through a gate removes the need to work out a fare before every journey.

Why fare calculation matters more than price

Buying a single ticket in Japan means knowing your destination's fare before you buy, from a chart above the machine, often in Japanese. It is entirely doable and it is a small tax on every journey. The card removes that step completely, which over a week is the real saving rather than the money.

Cards also work in convenience stores, vending machines and many small shops, so a balance is never stranded.

When a day pass wins

A Tokyo or Kyoto day pass starts to beat pay-as-you-go at roughly five rides in a single day, against individual fares of ¥180 to ¥330. Below that, the card is cheaper and simpler; above it, the pass pays and keeps paying, because every additional journey is free and the temptation to walk a tiring extra kilometre to save a fare disappears.

Tokyo

The Tokyo Subway Ticket, sold to visitors, costs ¥1,000 for twenty-four hours, with forty-eight and seventy-two hour versions above it. Its clock runs from the first time you pass a gate for a full twenty-four hours, not until midnight — activate it at eleven in the morning and it lasts until eleven the next morning.

The coverage trap: the tourist Tokyo Subway Ticket covers both the Tokyo Metro lines and the Toei lines. A separate, similarly named Tokyo Metro day ticket covers Metro only. Buying the wrong one leaves you at a gate that will not open on a route you assumed was included.

Kyoto

Kyoto's Subway and Bus One-Day Pass costs about ¥1,100 and covers all subway lines and the major city buses. Kyoto is a bus city more than a subway city, so a day of temple-hopping crosses the five-ride threshold easily and the pass is usually the right call there in a way it is not in Tokyo.

The long-standing bus-only day pass has been discontinued, which a great deal of English-language guidance still recommends. If a source tells you to buy it, that source has not been updated.

Two worked days

A Tokyo day spent in one district — a morning museum, lunch nearby, an afternoon walk, dinner in the same area — involves two rides. The card wins comfortably and the pass would waste most of its value.

A Tokyo day that crosses the city — an early market, a temple in the north-east, an afternoon in a western neighbourhood, dinner somewhere else again — involves six or seven. The pass wins, and the freedom to add an unplanned stop without recalculating is worth more than the money saved.

Kyoto behaves differently

Kyoto's sights are scattered around the edges of the city rather than concentrated along a subway spine, and the buses do most of the work of reaching them. A normal temple day in Kyoto crosses the five-ride threshold without trying, which is why the day pass is the usual answer there and the exception in Tokyo.

The tourist card option

Welcome Suica is a visitor card sold at Narita and Haneda and at major Tokyo stations. It needs no deposit and is valid for 28 days from purchase, which suits any normal trip. The catch is that the remaining balance is not refundable and it cannot be transferred to a phone, so load it in small increments.

An ordinary unregistered card is the better choice for anyone who might return, since the balance keeps and the deposit comes back.

Working out which applies to you

The test is simply how your days are shaped. Days that cluster around one neighbourhood and involve a lot of walking favour the card; days that criss-cross a city between scattered sights favour the pass. Most first trips contain both kinds, which is why the sensible approach is a card as the base and a day pass bought only on the days that earn it.

How those days get shaped in the first place — which sights cluster, which neighbourhood to base yourself in, how much a day can realistically hold — is the layer underneath this decision, and Japan, Worked Out works through it.
excerpt: Pay-as-you-go suits most first trips, but a day pass wins above roughly five rides. The prices, the coverage trap in Tokyo, and how to tell which applies to your day.

title: When Your IC Card Will Not Open the Gate: Fare Adjustment Explained
content:
The gate panels snap shut, a buzzer sounds, and a queue forms behind you. It is the single most stressful thirty seconds of a first trip on Japanese transit, and it is also completely routine — the machines that fix it stand a few metres away and the staff deal with it hundreds of times a day. This guide covers why the gate refuses you, how to clear it, and how to stop it happening again.

Why the gate refuses you

An insufficient balance causes most refusals, and Japanese gates deduct the fare on exit rather than on entry — so a Suica holding ¥120 will let you through at the start of a ¥300 journey and stop you dead at the other end. The card was never checked against the fare at the entry gate, because at that point the system did not know where you were going.

The other common causes

A card that was never tapped on entry produces the same result, which happens when a gate stands open during quiet periods and you walk through behind someone else. The system has no entry record, so it cannot compute a fare and refuses on principle. A card left unresolved from a previous journey — tapped in somewhere and never tapped out — does the same.

Read failures are the third category, and they are usually the wallet's fault rather than the card's. A tap that produces no beep at all, rather than a rejection buzz, is a reading problem.

The fare adjustment machine

Every station has a fare adjustment machine, and it sits on the platform side of the gates rather than beyond them — usually within a few metres of the barrier that just rejected you, often marked in English as well as Japanese. It exists precisely for this situation and using it takes well under a minute.

How to use it

Insert or tap the card, and the screen shows the shortfall. Feed in coins or a note, take the card back, and walk to the gate again. Most machines carry an English button in the corner of the screen, and the ones that do not still show the amount owed as a number, which is all you actually need to understand.

A standard top-up machine does the same job by a different route. If you would rather add a useful amount than pay an exact shortfall, top the card up normally and the gate will then deduct the fare and open.

If you have no cash

The staffed window beside the gates is the answer, and at any major station in Tokyo or Kyoto one attendant sits there whenever trains are running. Show the card, and the attendant resolves it — settling the fare, correcting a missing entry record, or waving you through if the fault was clearly the system's. It is an ordinary transaction rather than an escalation.

This is also the route for anything unusual: a card that will not read at all, a journey that crossed operators in a way the machine will not resolve, or a balance dispute. The counter has authority the machine does not.

The bus rule that catches people out

City buses in Kyoto do not all work the way the trains do, and the difference produces a fare that looks wrong rather than a gate that closes. On most Kyoto city routes you tap once on boarding and pay one flat fare; elsewhere, and on longer suburban routes, you tap on entry and again on exit so the distance can be calculated. Missing the second tap leaves the journey open.

What an open journey does

An unresolved bus or rail journey can charge the maximum fare for the line, or leave the card in a state the next gate refuses. The fix is the same as any other adjustment — the driver resolves it on the bus, or a station machine or counter clears it afterwards — but the cause is invisible if you did not know a second tap existed.

When in doubt, watch what the person ahead of you does. Japanese transit is full of small local conventions like this, and the queue demonstrates them for free.

The two-card problem

Carrying two contactless cards in one wallet is the most common cause of a Suica tap that produces no response at all. The reader sees two cards, cannot decide which to charge, and reads neither. A hotel key card, an office badge or a contactless bank card sitting against a Suica will all do it.

The fix

Take the card out of the wallet and tap it on its own. If that works, the wallet was the problem. Travellers who tap a whole wallet for a fortnight without incident sometimes hit this on day twelve because a new card went in that morning, which is why the symptom feels random.

A phone in a case with cards tucked behind it produces the same failure, and it is worth knowing before you are standing at a gate trying to work out whether your phone has broken.

Keeping it from happening

Keep about ¥2,000 on the card as a working floor rather than running it to zero, because that clears any single city journey without thought, and topping up at that point costs nothing but a machine stop you were going to make anyway. The maximum a card holds is ¥20,000, so there is plenty of headroom.

Why not simply load the maximum

Because the balance is easier to spend down than to recover. An unregistered card can be refunded at the issuing operator's stations with the ¥500 deposit returned, but a handling fee applies and the process takes a counter visit on a day you would rather be doing something else. Load enough to be comfortable, not enough to strand money.

Tap deliberately rather than quickly — a flat, firm contact for a full second, held rather than swiped. Most read failures on a working card are a tap that moved.

If the card is lost

An unregistered Suica is cash: losing it loses the balance and the ¥500 deposit with no recourse, because the card carries no name and the operator cannot connect it to you. A registered card, by contrast, can be cancelled and reissued with the remaining balance transferred, which is the practical argument for registering one if the option is offered at purchase.

A card held in a phone sits in a different category again, protected by the device's own lock and recoverable through the account it was created under. For most visitors on a short trip the unregistered card is still the sensible choice; the point is simply to treat it like the cash it is rather than like a bank card that can be frozen.

The thirty seconds in perspective

A refused gate is a routine event that Japanese commuters clear several times a year without embarrassment, and the infrastructure assumes it will happen. Step aside, use the machine, and rejoin — nobody behind you is surprised and the staff have seen it all morning.

Getting the card right at the start removes most of these moments before they occur, and where that sits in the order of everything else to set up before arrival is something Japan, Worked Out works through.
