title: Mobile Suica on an American iPhone: Setup and Limits
content:
A transit card on your phone is the single most useful thing an American visitor can set up before flying to Japan, and it works better than most people expect. It also fails in one specific, poorly documented way that leaves travellers stuck at a ticket gate. This guide covers the setup, the card that will not work, and what to do instead.

It works on a US iPhone, with no Japanese account

Suica and Pasmo can be added to Apple Wallet on an iPhone bought in the United States, on iPhone 8 or later and Apple Watch Series 3 or later. You do not need a Japanese Apple ID, and you do not need to change your App Store region. The card is created inside Wallet, and it can be set up before you leave home.

The misconception worth killing

A great deal of older advice insists you need a Japanese Apple ID, a Japanese address, or the Japanese version of an app. That has not been true for years, and following it sends people down a pointless and occasionally risky detour involving second accounts. Wallet, Transit Card, Suica — that is the whole path.

Once created, the card runs in Express Mode, which means you tap the gate without unlocking the phone or opening anything. It keeps working when the battery is low.

The part that actually goes wrong

Topping up a mobile Suica inside Apple Wallet will not accept a US-issued Visa card. American Express and Mastercard issued in the United States do work. This is the single most common point of failure for American visitors, and it produces a confusing error rather than an explanation.

Two sharper details

A US-issued Mastercard works for Suica but not for Pasmo, so if you have a choice of which card to create, Suica is the more forgiving one. And where Wallet refuses a card outright, the separate Suica app will sometimes accept the same card — an inconsistency with no official explanation, but a working escape route.

There is also a nightly maintenance window, running until roughly four in the morning Japan time, during which top-ups fail for everybody regardless of card. A failure at two in the morning is not a card problem, and retrying after the window usually resolves it.

What to do before you fly

Set the Suica up at home before you leave the United States, load a modest amount, and confirm a top-up actually completes with the card you intend to use. Discovering that your only card is refused is far better done on your sofa than at a gate in Shinjuku with a queue behind you.

The maximum balance is ¥20,000, which is more than enough for a week of city transit. Top up in small amounts rather than loading the maximum, because the balance is easier to spend down than to recover.

If you are on Android

Mobile Suica on Android requires Osaifu-Keitai, the hardware and software stack fitted to Japanese-market handsets. Android phones sold outside Japan almost universally lack it and cannot add a Suica or Pasmo, no matter which app is installed. This is a hardware limitation, not a settings problem.

The answer for Android users is a physical card, which is straightforward again: unregistered Suica and Pasmo cards returned to sale in March 2025 and are bought from station machines with a ¥500 refundable deposit plus whatever you load.

If you are already in Japan and stuck

Arriving without a working top-up method is recoverable and common enough that stations are set up for it. A physical card bought from a machine takes cash, which sidesteps the entire card-network problem in one step, and the machines at every major station carry English interfaces.

Cash top-ups also work on a card already in your wallet, at any station machine and at convenience-store registers. If the phone refuses your credit card, the answer is not to keep retrying it — it is to feed the card cash and move on.

Apple Watch is worth setting up too

A Suica on a paired Apple Watch works at gates independently of the phone, which is genuinely useful when the phone is in a bag and both hands are full. The card lives on one device at a time, so decide which before you travel rather than at a gate.

Where the card actually works

Suica, Pasmo and Icoca have been mutually interoperable nationwide since 2013, so a card created in Tokyo works on Kyoto and Osaka transit without any change. It also works as a payment card in convenience stores, vending machines and many small shops, which is genuinely useful in a country where cash still matters.

A handful of smaller regional operators and rural bus routes sit outside the scheme. In the cities a first trip visits, that is not a practical constraint.

What the card decision connects to

Notice what this one small setup actually touched. Which card you can top up with determines whether the phone works at all, which determines whether you need a physical card, which determines whether you need cash on arrival — and that last one runs straight into how you get money in Japan at all, which is its own tangle of ATMs that reject foreign cards.

Each of those is usually solved separately, at the airport, under time pressure, with luggage. They are one connected problem with a sensible order to solve it in, and working out that order in advance is what Japan, Worked Out is built for.
excerpt: You can add a Suica to a US iPhone without a Japanese Apple ID. The part that catches Americans out is which card tops it up — and one network is refused outright.

title: How to Navigate Japanese Train Stations
content:
Japan's major train stations can be vast and bustling — small cities in themselves, with multiple levels, dozens of exits, and hundreds of thousands of passengers a day. But they're remarkably well organized, clean, and signed, and with a few tips, navigating them becomes second nature within a day or two. Here's how to move through them confidently, even jet-lagged and hauling luggage.

Signs are your friend (and in English)

Major stations have clear English signage throughout, alongside Japanese — with color-coded lines, directional arrows, platform numbers, and station numbers. Follow the signs for your line (identified by its color and letter) and your direction of travel. Large electronic boards display upcoming train times, platforms, and destinations, cycling through English. Once you learn to follow the color of your line, even a huge station becomes a matter of following arrows.

Finding your platform

  • Use a transit app to know your line, direction, and platform number before you enter — this is the single biggest time-saver.
  • Follow signage to the correct line, then to the correct platform for your direction (endpoints/destinations are signed, so know which way you're heading).
  • Platform displays show the next trains, their type (local, rapid, express, limited express), and which stations they stop at — check the type, as faster trains skip stations and you don't want to overshoot or get left behind.
  • Floor markings show exactly where each door will open and where to queue.

The exit matters — a lot

The exit is the biggest first-timer lesson: large stations have many exits, sometimes dozens, spread across a wide area and even different sides of a district. Taking the wrong one can mean a 10–15 minute detour or a long walk back around. Know your exit name or number in advance — your map app or directions will usually specify it (e.g. "Hachiko Exit," "East Exit," or a numbered exit like "Exit A3"). Follow the signs to that specific exit. When in doubt, large maps near the gates show all exits and what's near each.

Using your IC card

Tap your IC card (Suica, Pasmo, ICOCA, etc.) on the reader at the ticket gates to enter and exit — the gate opens and the correct fare is deducted automatically, no ticket required. If your balance is too low to exit, don't panic: use a fare-adjustment (seisanki) machine near the gates to top up before tapping out. Keep the card somewhere easily accessible, since you'll be tapping frequently throughout the day. Note that you generally can't ride between separate IC "areas" (e.g. far intercity stretches) on the card alone, and limited-express or Shinkansen trains need a separate ticket.

Helpful station facilities

  • Coin lockers: widely available in various sizes for storing luggage while you explore — many now take IC cards. Perfect for day trips or the gap before hotel check-in. (They fill up at busy stations, so grab one early.)
  • Restrooms: clean, free, and found throughout stations.
  • Convenience stores, bakeries, and food: stations are packed with shops, bento, ekiben, and eateries — often a great quick meal.
  • Information counters and staff: staff at major stations can help, and many speak some English; don't hesitate to ask or point to your destination.
  • Luggage forwarding (takkyubin) counters at some stations can send bags ahead to your next hotel.

Tips for a smooth experience

  • Allow extra time at big stations, especially for transfers — walking distances between lines can be surprisingly long.
  • Avoid rush hour (roughly 8–9am and 6–7pm on weekdays) with luggage if you possibly can — the busiest lines get extremely packed.
  • Stand on the correct side of escalators (the standing side varies by region — left in Tokyo, right in Osaka — so just observe and follow the locals), leaving the other side clear for walkers.
  • Keep with the flow of foot traffic and don't stop suddenly in busy passages; step to the side to check your phone or map.
  • For the Shinkansen, there are separate gates and platforms — follow the dedicated bullet-train signs.
  • Let passengers off the train first before boarding, and line up on the platform markings.

The mega-stations worth knowing in advance

A handful of stations are large enough to deserve a specific mention: Shinjuku (the world's busiest, over 200 exits), Tokyo Station (a maze of underground passages linking Shinkansen, JR, and subway lines), and Kyoto Station (large but far simpler, essentially one long concourse). If your itinerary routes you through any of these for a transfer, budget extra time on that leg specifically rather than assuming a station transfer takes the same few minutes everywhere.

Bottom line

Japanese stations are big but deeply logical. Lean on a transit app, follow the excellent English signage and line colors, know your exit before you arrive, tap through with your IC card, and make use of the lockers, food, and facilities. A little preparation turns even the most daunting mega-station into easy, navigable territory — and the efficiency quickly becomes one of the quiet joys of traveling in Japan. Getting comfortable with stations matters most on the days your itinerary asks the most of them — the transfer days between cities — which is exactly what Japan, Worked Out is built to plan around.
excerpt: Big Japanese stations can overwhelm first-timers. Here's how to find your platform, exit, and way through, plus lockers, signs, and tips.

title: Suica vs Pasmo: Japan IC Card Guide
content:
An IC card is the single most useful thing to get when you arrive in Japan. These rechargeable tap cards make trains, subways, and buses effortless — and you can use them to pay at convenience stores, vending machines, lockers, and many shops too. For a first-timer, getting one is the best five minutes you'll spend on arrival. Here's everything you need to know.

What an IC card is

An IC card is a prepaid, rechargeable smart card you simply tap on readers to ride public transit and make small purchases. There's no need to calculate fares or buy individual paper tickets — you tap in when you enter a station, tap out when you leave, and the correct fare is deducted automatically. It turns Japan's complex web of train and bus operators into one seamless tap-and-go experience, and it's accepted almost everywhere a traveler goes.

Suica vs Pasmo: what's the difference?

The two best-known cards are Suica and Pasmo. For a traveler they are functionally almost identical — both work interchangeably across trains, subways, and buses in the Tokyo area and, thanks to nationwide IC compatibility, in most major cities across Japan. The difference is mainly the issuing company (Suica is from JR East; Pasmo from the private railways and subways). Pick whichever you can get easily; for travel purposes they behave the same. There are also regional equivalents — most notably ICOCA in the Kansai/Kyoto/Osaka area — which are similarly interchangeable for most travel nationwide.

Good news: cards are easy to buy again

You may have read that Suica and Pasmo were hard to get due to a global semiconductor shortage that limited card production. That restriction ended in March 2025 — standard cards are once again readily sold at airport stations and major station ticket machines, so you no longer need to worry about them being unavailable. A few options to know:

  • Standard Suica/Pasmo: buy at ticket machines (with an English option) or counters; they carry a small refundable deposit and don't expire as long as they're used periodically.
  • Welcome Suica (and tourist Pasmo Passport): visitor-oriented cards with no deposit, valid for 28 days from first use — handy for a short trip, though any leftover balance isn't refunded.
  • Mobile/digital IC cards: you can add Suica or Pasmo to a phone wallet on supported devices and recharge with a card — no physical card needed. There's also a Welcome Suica Mobile app aimed at overseas visitors.

How to get one

  • Buy at ticket machines in train and subway stations (including right at the airport station) or at staffed counters.
  • Load it with cash at the machine (English menus available); some machines also take cards.
  • Choose a physical card, a tourist version, or add a digital one to your phone if supported.
  • Get one as soon as you arrive — at the airport station or your first train station — so transit is sorted from minute one.

How to use it

  • Transit: tap on the reader at the gate when entering, and tap again when exiting; the fare is automatic. On buses, tap when boarding and (usually) again when alighting.
  • Shopping: tap to pay at convenience stores, vending machines, many shops and restaurants, and station lockers — a fast, cashless convenience.
  • Recharge (chage): top up with cash at any station machine when the balance runs low; keep a positive balance, since you can't exit a gate with insufficient funds (use a fare-adjustment machine if caught short).

Good to know: the limits

IC cards are brilliant for everyday city and regional transit, but a couple of limits are worth understanding. You generally can't ride across separate IC "areas" in one tap (for long intercity journeys the system won't let you tap out far away on a single ride), and the card doesn't cover limited-express or Shinkansen travel — trains like the Narita Express, Keisei Skyliner, and the Haruka airport express, and all bullet trains, need their own separate ticket. For those, buy the ticket separately; the IC card is for the ordinary local and regional trains, subways, and buses.

Where this fits into your bigger transit plan

Getting an IC card sorted is the easy part of Japan transit — it's a five-minute errand with almost no wrong choices. The harder decision most first-timers actually face is what to pair it with: whether a Japan Rail Pass makes sense for your specific route, and where the line falls between rides your IC card covers and the longer-distance Shinkansen hops it doesn't. Get the IC card sorted first, since it's zero-risk and instant, then work out the pass math separately — Japan, Worked Out walks through exactly how the two fit together for different itinerary shapes.

Practical tips

  • One card per person — you generally can't pass one card back through a gate for two people.
  • Children can have their own card with children's fares applied.
  • Keep it handy — in a phone case or easy pocket — since you'll tap constantly.
  • Leftover balance can be spent on purchases; standard cards can often be refunded at a JR/operator counter (sometimes minus a small fee), but many travelers just spend it down at a convenience store before leaving.
  • A digital card on your phone avoids the deposit and refund hassle entirely, if your device supports it.

Bottom line

Whether you get a Suica, Pasmo, ICOCA, or a digital version on your phone, an IC card is an absolute must — and they're easy to buy again now that the shortage has ended. Grab one on arrival, keep it topped up, tap your way effortlessly through Japan's trains, subways, buses, and shops, and just remember to buy separate tickets for the Shinkansen and airport express trains.
excerpt: IC cards like Suica and Pasmo make Japan's transit effortless. Here's what they are, the difference, how to get one, and how to use it.

title: Tokyo Subway and Train System Explained
content:
Tokyo's rail network is one of the most extensive and efficient on earth — and, at first glance, one of the most intimidating maps you'll ever see, a tangle of colored lines run by multiple companies. But it's logical, exceptionally well-signed in English, and genuinely easy once you grasp a few basics. Here's how to navigate it without stress.

The key players

Tokyo's network is run by several different operators, which is why the map looks so busy:

  • JR (Japan Railways) East: runs the above-ground lines, most famously the Yamanote loop that circles central Tokyo, plus other useful lines like the Chuo and Sobu.
  • Tokyo Metro and Toei: the two subway systems that web the city underground (Tokyo Metro is the larger; Toei the other).
  • Private railways: several companies (Keio, Odakyu, Tokyu, Keisei, Keikyu, and more) reaching the suburbs, the airports, and day-trip destinations.

The crucial point for travelers: your IC card (Suica/Pasmo) works across all of them with a single tap, so you rarely need to think about which company runs a given line — just tap in and out.

The Yamanote line: your anchor

The JR Yamanote line is the green loop that connects most major districts — Tokyo Station, Shinjuku, Shibuya, Harajuku, Ikebukuro, Ueno, and more — in a big circle around the city center. It's the mental map that makes Tokyo click: many of the sights and hotels you'll care about are on or near it, and you can simply ride the loop around to them. For getting across the middle of the circle, the Metro subway lines cut through. Yamanote loop plus Metro covers the vast majority of a first-timer's needs.

How to navigate

  • Use a mapping or transit app — it gives you exact routes, transfer points, platforms, travel times, fares, and which exit to use. This is by far the single biggest help; trust it and follow step by step.
  • Follow the color-coded lines and station numbers — each line has a color and letter, and each station a number (e.g. G-09), which makes following routes and transfers easy even without reading Japanese.
  • Signs, maps, and announcements are in English on all major lines.
  • Tap in and out with your IC card; fares are automatic, so you don't pre-calculate anything.

Tips for big stations

Major hubs like Shinjuku (the world's busiest station), Tokyo, and Shibuya are enormous, multi-level, and have many exits. The trick: know your exit name or number before you arrive (your app will tell you), since choosing the right one can save a long detour. Allow extra time for transfers, as walking between lines can take several minutes. If you get turned around, follow signs toward a known landmark or simply surface and reorient with your map — it happens to everyone at first.

Rush hour

Trains are punctual and frequent but get extremely crowded during rush hours — roughly 8–9am and 6–7pm on weekdays, when the busiest lines are famously packed (you've seen the videos). Avoid traveling with large luggage at these times if you can, and be prepared to be pressed in shoulder-to-shoulder on the worst stretches. Off-peak and weekends are far more comfortable, and there are sometimes women-only cars during rush hour (marked on the platform).

Practical notes

  • Trains generally stop running around midnight and resume early morning — plan late nights around the last train, or budget for a taxi.
  • Keep quiet, set your phone to silent (manner mode), and don't take calls on the train.
  • Queue on the platform markings and let passengers off before boarding.
  • Priority seats are for the elderly, pregnant, injured, or those with small children — leave them free if you don't need them.
  • Eating is generally avoided on local/commuter trains (it's fine on long-distance/Shinkansen).

Fares and passes for a short stay

For most first-time visitors, paying per ride with an IC card works out simpler and often cheaper than a multi-day subway pass, since a mixed day of Yamanote + Metro + occasional private-line trips doesn't map cleanly onto any single pass's coverage. Tokyo Metro and Toei each sell their own day passes, plus a combined one covering both, but they only pay off if you're riding many short subway hops in a single day and rarely touching JR lines — check the math against your actual planned stops before buying one instead of just tapping as you go.

Bottom line

Don't let the map scare you. With an IC card in your pocket, a transit app in your hand, and the Yamanote loop as your mental anchor, Tokyo's trains are fast, spotless, reliable, and surprisingly easy to use. A little practice on day one and you'll be zipping around the city like a local by day two — and once Tokyo clicks, the same tap-and-go logic carries over to every other city on a well-sequenced route, which Japan, Worked Out maps out beyond just Tokyo.
excerpt: Tokyo's train network looks daunting but is logical and efficient. Here's how to navigate the subway, JR lines, and the Yamanote loop.

title: Flights to Japan from the US: Routes, Times & Booking Tips
content:
Getting to Japan from the US is more straightforward than the distance suggests. Multiple nonstop routes connect major American hubs to Tokyo and Osaka, served by both US and Japanese carriers, and the flight — while long — is very manageable, especially if you plan the timing to your advantage. Here's what to know about routes, flight times, costs, and booking smart.

Which airports you'll fly into

Japan has three main international gateways for US travelers: Tokyo Haneda (HND), Tokyo Narita (NRT), and Osaka Kansai (KIX). Haneda sits much closer to central Tokyo than Narita, so if you're starting in Tokyo and have the choice, flying into Haneda usually saves you time and money on the airport transfer. Kansai (KIX) is the natural choice if you're beginning your trip in Kyoto or Osaka, letting you skip a backtrack from Tokyo. A fourth option worth knowing about: some itineraries route through a connecting hub like Seoul (ICN) or Taipei (TPE) on a partner or budget carrier, which can undercut nonstop fares by a meaningful margin in exchange for a longer travel day — worth pricing out if your dates are flexible and you don't mind an extra stop.

Nonstop routes from the US

You can fly nonstop to Japan from a wide range of US cities, including Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Portland, Las Vegas, Chicago, Detroit, Minneapolis, Houston, Dallas, Atlanta, New York/Newark, Boston, and Washington Dulles, among others. The two Japanese carriers — Japan Airlines (JAL) and ANA, both consistently top-rated — fly these routes alongside the major US airlines (United, American, Delta), so there's usually solid competition on price and schedule. Smaller or inland cities typically connect through a West Coast hub.

How long is the flight?

Flight time depends heavily on which coast you leave from:

  • West Coast (LAX, SFO, SEA): roughly 11–12 hours nonstop.
  • East Coast (JFK/EWR, IAD, BOS): roughly 13–14 hours nonstop.
  • Central hubs (ORD, DFW): somewhere in between.

Returning to the US is often a bit longer due to headwinds. Japan is well ahead of every US time zone (it's a day "ahead" across the Pacific), so the time change is significant — build in a buffer day at the start of your trip to shake off the jet lag before diving into sightseeing.

Making the long flight more bearable

A few practical choices matter more on an 11+ hour flight than a domestic one. An aisle seat trades window views for the freedom to get up without climbing over a stranger, which most people prefer on an overnight leg. If your budget allows it, premium economy on the Japanese carriers is a genuinely different experience from US carriers' version — more recline, a footrest, and better food — and can be worth pricing against a coach fare with a paid upgrade. Set your watch to Japan time as soon as you board, sleep on the segment of the flight that aligns with Japan nighttime, and skip the alcohol; it makes jet lag meaningfully worse on a flight this long.

What flights cost

Fares to Japan swing a lot by season, route, and how far ahead you book. Cherry blossom season (late March–April) and the fall foliage months (October–November) tend to be the most expensive and competitive, so they reward booking early — often several months out, realistically 4 to 6 months for the best fares in those windows versus 2 to 3 for shoulder-season travel. Rather than quote a figure that goes stale, it's best to compare live fares across a range of dates; a flexible-date search quickly reveals which travel weeks are cheapest, and shoulder seasons or winter (outside the holidays) often deliver the best deals. This is a good place to run a quick flight search from the US and watch a few dates before committing. (This article contains affiliate links — if you book through them we earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.)

Booking tips

Be flexible on your gateway

If you're not locked into Tokyo, pricing Haneda, Narita, and Kansai separately can surface a meaningfully cheaper fare. You can even fly into one city and out of another — an "open-jaw" ticket — which is ideal if your itinerary runs Tokyo to Kyoto, since you can depart from Kansai instead of backtracking to Tokyo. This often costs little or no more than a round trip and saves a travel day, and it's usually the single biggest lever on how well the rest of your route flows — exactly how many cities to string together and in what order is its own decision worth getting right before you lock in flights, which Japan, Worked Out walks through in more depth.

Watch the peak windows

Aim to book well ahead for late March–April and October–November. Try to avoid Japan's domestic holiday crunches like Golden Week (late April–early May), Obon (mid-August), and New Year, which spike both airfare and crowds.

Consider the arrival time

An afternoon or evening arrival makes it easiest to head straight to your hotel and sleep, which helps reset your body clock. A morning arrival means a long first day fighting to stay awake — doable, but plan something light, and if you do land early, resist the urge to nap for more than an hour or two; a long daytime nap on day one is what usually turns a one-day adjustment into three.

Mind your gateway vs your route

Match your arrival and departure airports to your itinerary's shape — into Tokyo, out of Kansai (or vice versa) for the classic Tokyo–Kyoto trip — to avoid wasting time backtracking.

Bottom line

Nonstop service from both US coasts makes Japan an easy long-haul to plan. Pick your gateway based on where your trip begins, search flexible dates to catch a good fare, consider an open-jaw ticket to save backtracking, and give yourself an easy first day on the ground to beat the jet lag. With your flights set, the next questions are usually entry requirements and what to expect on arrival.

title: Money in Japan: Cash, Cards & IC Cards Explained
content:
Money in Japan trips up a lot of first-time American visitors, because the country is more cash-oriented than the US — even though it feels ultra-modern in every other way. The good news is that the system is simple once you understand it, and a little preparation means you'll never be caught short. Here's how to pay for things smoothly.

Cash still matters

Credit cards are widely accepted in cities, hotels, department stores, chain restaurants, and tourist spots — and card acceptance keeps growing. But plenty of small restaurants, neighborhood shops, market stalls, temples and shrines (for entry fees and charms), and rural businesses still take cash only. The rule of thumb: always carry more yen than you think you'll need, and top up before heading into smaller towns or the countryside — that's also where the reliable foreign-card ATMs thin out fastest, a gap Japan, Worked Out plans around city by city. Japan is extremely safe, so carrying a fair amount of cash isn't the worry it might be elsewhere — pickpocketing is rare.

The currency

Japan uses the Japanese yen (¥), in coins (¥1 up to ¥500) and notes (¥1,000 up to ¥10,000). Exchange rates move constantly, so check the current USD-to-yen rate close to your trip rather than relying on an old figure — a quick mental conversion at the day's rate saves you from sticker shock or accidental overspending. Coins add up fast here (the ¥500 coin is worth several dollars), so a coin purse is genuinely useful, and IC cards help absorb your small change.

Getting yen: use the right ATMs

The easiest way to get cash is withdrawing from an ATM with your US debit card once you arrive — the rate is usually better than airport currency-exchange desks. The catch is that not every Japanese ATM accepts foreign cards. The reliable ones are:

  • 7-Eleven (Seven Bank) ATMs — inside their convenience stores, which are everywhere, open 24/7, and have English menus.
  • Japan Post Bank ATMs — at post offices nationwide, also foreign-card friendly with English support.

Both consistently accept foreign Visa, Mastercard, and other major cards. Tell your bank you're traveling so the card isn't frozen — a genuinely common trip-ruining mistake that's entirely avoidable with one phone call beforehand — and check your withdrawal and foreign-transaction fees before you go; many travel-focused cards waive the latter, but plenty of everyday cards charge 1–3% on every purchase, which adds up over a two-week trip.

IC cards: your transit lifeline (and a wallet)

An IC card — Suica, Pasmo, or the Kansai ICOCA — is the one piece of "money" advice that matters most day to day: a rechargeable tap card you'll use constantly for trains, subways, and buses, and you can also tap it to pay at convenience stores, vending machines, coin lockers, and many shops and restaurants. Load it with cash at any station machine and simply tap in and out. It turns the transit system from confusing to effortless and soaks up your small change into easy cashless payments. Get one as soon as you land — they're easy to buy again now that a past production shortage has ended, and you can even add a digital version to a supported phone.

Tipping: don't

Here's the big cultural shift for Americans: there is no tipping in Japan. Service — which is famously attentive — is already included in the price, and leaving extra cash can actually cause confusion or be politely refused (staff may chase you to return it). This applies across the board: restaurants, taxis, hotels, salons, everywhere. Don't tip; it isn't rude, it's simply not the custom. This alone can simplify (and slightly cheapen) your trip versus home.

How much to budget

Daily costs vary widely by travel style — from budget travelers eating at convenience stores and ramen counters and riding trains, to mid-range travelers in business hotels, to higher-end stays in ryokan with kaiseki dinners. Japan can be surprisingly affordable day to day (a great ramen lunch costs only a few dollars, and konbini meals are cheap and good), while rail travel and nicer hotels are where budgets climb. Because prices and exchange rates shift, it's best to price your specific hotels, Shinkansen legs, and meals at current rates rather than lock in a fixed daily number.

Tax-free shopping is changing in late 2026

Japan's tax-free shopping system for tourists changes on November 1, 2026 — worth knowing if your trip straddles that date. Through October 31, 2026, eligible visitors get the roughly 10% consumption tax (8% on food and non-alcoholic drinks) taken off at the register or refunded on the spot at a store's tax-free counter, generally on purchases of at least ¥5,000 before tax at the same store on the same day. From November 1, 2026 onward, everyone pays the tax-inclusive price at checkout and claims the refund later at the airport before departure, within 90 days of the purchase. Either way, keep your passport on you when shopping and your receipts until you leave the country — and note that since April 2025, items shipped home internationally no longer qualify; you have to carry the purchase out with you.

Customs note

If you're carrying very large sums, be aware that Japan requires you to declare amounts over the equivalent of about ¥1,000,000 at customs (combining cash and certain instruments). Most travelers never come anywhere close, so this rarely applies.

Bottom line

Carry plenty of cash, get a Suica or Pasmo on arrival, use 7-Eleven or Japan Post ATMs for withdrawals, tell your bank you're traveling, and forget everything you know about tipping. Sort those out and the money side of your trip basically runs itself — leaving you free to focus on where to go and when.
excerpt: Japan is more cash-friendly than the US. Here is how to pay, where US cards work, which ATMs to use, the late-2026 tax-free shopping change, and why you do not tip.

title: Autumn Foliage in Japan: Timing Your Trip
content:
Autumn is Japan's other great season, and for a first trip it is the more forgiving one. The colour lasts weeks rather than days, the weather is settled, and the timing is far more predictable than spring. This guide covers when the colour peaks where, how to plan around it, and where to see it without standing in the worst of the crowds.

When the colour peaks, region by region

Autumn colour peaks in Hokkaido and the Japanese Alps during October, in Kyoto through the second half of November, and in Tokyo from late November into the first days of December. The colour moves in the opposite direction to the cherry blossom — north to south, and from high ground down into the valleys and cities.

Reading the direction of travel

That north-to-south, high-to-low movement is genuinely useful for planning. If you are in Japan in late October, the mountains are already turning while Kyoto is still green. Arrive in the third week of November and the cities are at their best while the high country is bare. A trip that moves from the mountains toward the cities over a fortnight can effectively follow the colour down.

Why autumn is easier to plan than spring

Autumn foliage in Kyoto or Tokyo holds for several weeks in a given place, where cherry blossom holds for roughly one. That difference changes everything about the booking problem. A spring trip is a bet on a seven-day window that nobody can forecast until February; an autumn trip aimed at the back half of November is very likely to land on good colour regardless of how the year has gone.

The weather helps as well. Late autumn in Japan is reliably clear and cool, with far less rain than early summer and none of the heat that makes August walking difficult. For a trip built around being outdoors, it is the most comfortable stretch of the year.

Where the crowds actually are

Autumn crowding in Kyoto during the last ten days of November behaves much like spring crowding: it concentrates in a small number of celebrated places rather than spreading out. Kyoto's most famous temple gardens in the last ten days of November are genuinely difficult, with queues at the gate and paths moving at a shuffle. Fifteen minutes away, less-photographed temples carry the same maples and a tenth of the people.

Two things reliably help. Go early, because the famous gardens open before the tour groups reach them. And go up — hillside temples and walking routes thin out quickly, because most visitors will not climb for a view they can photograph from the flat.

The evening illuminations

Many temples run special evening openings during the colour season, lighting the maples after dark. They are beautiful and they are extremely popular, so treat them as their own outing rather than something you append to a full day of sightseeing. If you plan to do one, it is worth building the day around it.

Colour beyond the famous gardens

Autumn colour in Japan is not confined to the temple gardens that appear in every photograph. City parks, riverbanks, university campuses and the approach roads to ordinary shrines carry the same maples, and the mountains around Kyoto and Tokyo are within reach of a half-day walk. A trip that treats the celebrated gardens as one item among several, rather than the whole point, tends to see more colour and stand in fewer queues.

What to book, and when

Autumn does not demand spring's six-month lead, but the back half of November in Kyoto is one of the busiest lodging periods of the year and behaves accordingly. Rooms in central Kyoto get expensive and scarce; reserved seats on the fast trains fill on the main corridors at weekends. Two to three months ahead is usually comfortable, and earlier if you want a specific traditional inn.

Booking pressure is one of several ways the calendar quietly shapes a first trip — how many bases you can use, which cities work at which times, and how much of the route you can commit to before you know the weather. Japan, Worked Out works through how those pieces interact.

Autumn against spring, as a decision

Put Japan's two peak seasons side by side — a one-week bloom window in late March and early April against several weeks of colour from October to early December — and the choice becomes clearer than the marketing suggests. Spring offers a shorter, more dramatic spectacle on a window nobody can forecast in time to book. Autumn offers a longer, steadier one on a window you can plan around months ahead.

Spring wins on the strength of the image and on the atmosphere — the whole country is out under the trees, and there is nothing else quite like it. Autumn wins on almost everything practical: settled weather, a forgiving timetable, a shorter booking lead, and prices that, while high in Kyoto, do not reach spring's peaks across the board.

For a first trip where the cities and the routing are themselves new, the season that does not also demand a gamble is the easier one to build a plan on. For a return trip with a specific image in mind, spring's risk is worth taking.

Combining colour with the rest of a trip

Autumn's several-week span in Kyoto and Tokyo, against cherry blossom's single week, is what makes November easy to combine with everything else. Because you are not chasing a seven-day window, you can plan a normal route through the country and let the colour meet you along the way. A standard first week through Tokyo and Kyoto needs no adjustment at all in mid-November beyond booking earlier than you otherwise would.

The one date to keep an eye on is the very end of November in Kyoto, when the city is at its absolute peak and at its most crowded. If you would rather have the gardens than the photograph, aim a week either side.
excerpt: Autumn colour moves from Hokkaido in October to Kyoto in late November. The regional timetable, why it is easier to plan than spring, and where to see it without the worst crowds.

title: Best Time to Visit Japan (and When to Avoid)
content:
Japan is a genuine four-season destination, and the time you choose shapes the entire trip — from cherry blossoms to fiery autumn maples to powder snow. There's no single "best" time, but there are clear standouts and a few periods worth avoiding. Here's how the seasons break down, what each offers, and the specific dates to steer around.

The two best windows

If you can pick your dates freely, two windows stand out above the rest:

  • Late March to April — cherry blossom (sakura) season. Mild weather and the iconic pink blooms make this the most celebrated and romantic time to visit, with a festive atmosphere as the whole country turns out for hanami (blossom viewing). The trade-off: it's the busiest and priciest season, and the exact bloom timing shifts year to year, so book early and stay flexible.
  • October to November — autumn foliage (koyo). Crisp, comfortable, clear weather and brilliant fall colors, especially stunning in Kyoto's temple gardens. Many seasoned travelers consider this the genuine sweet spot — gorgeous scenery with slightly easier logistics and weather than spring.

Season by season

Spring (March–May)

Mild and beautiful, anchored by the cherry blossoms. The bloom moves south to north over several weeks and varies year to year, so a little date flexibility helps if sakura are your goal. Late spring (after the blossoms, before the rains) is pleasant and a bit quieter, aside from the Golden Week holiday cluster.

Summer (June–August)

Hot and increasingly humid, with a rainy season (tsuyu) typically through June into mid-July across much of the country, and the start of typhoon season later. August brings real heat and humidity. It's still very doable — summer is the time of vibrant festivals (matsuri), fireworks, and lush green landscapes, and the mountains and northern Hokkaido stay cooler — but it's the least comfortable stretch weather-wise.

Fall (September–November)

Once the summer heat and early-autumn typhoon risk ease, fall turns mild and clear, finishing with spectacular autumn colors from late October into November. Comfortable temperatures and beautiful scenery make it an excellent and slightly underrated time to go.

Winter (December–February)

Cold, with serious snow in the north and along the Japan Sea coast — superb for skiing (Hokkaido's powder is world-famous) and for soaking in steaming outdoor onsen surrounded by snow. Tokyo and Kyoto stay chilly but mostly snow-light and sunny, illuminations brighten the cities, and — outside the New Year period — crowds are thinner and prices lower. An underrated season for the big cities.

Periods to avoid

Some dates are crowded, expensive, or weather-challenged. Try to steer around:

  • Golden Week (late April to early May) — a cluster of national holidays when domestic travel surges, prices spike, trains fill, and popular spots overflow. The single biggest one to avoid if you can.
  • Obon (around mid-August) — a major holiday when many Japanese travel to their hometowns; transport and lodging get busy and pricey.
  • New Year (roughly Dec 29–Jan 3) — many businesses and restaurants close, and trains fill with people traveling home; atmospheric for shrine visits but logistically tricky.
  • June to mid-July rainy season — frequent rain (though it has its own lush charm and fewer crowds).
  • Peak August — intense heat, humidity, and rising typhoon risk that can disrupt flights and trains.

A note on cherry blossom timing

Because the sakura bloom is brief (often just a week or so at a given spot) and the dates shift annually with the weather, chasing it requires some luck and flexibility. Forecasts are published in the months beforehand. If blossoms are your priority, build in a few days of buffer and be ready to travel south or to higher elevations to catch them — the bloom front moves predictably northward and upward.

How your dates ripple into the rest of the trip

Picking a season isn't an isolated decision — it changes what the rest of your planning should look like. Traveling during Golden Week or peak cherry blossom means booking accommodation and any timed tickets (teamLab, popular restaurants) far earlier than you'd otherwise need to, and it may push you toward fewer, more locked-in day trips rather than a flexible day-by-day plan. A winter trip opens up cheaper, less crowded cities but narrows out mountain day trips unless skiing is the point. None of that is obvious from the season alone — it only shows up once you're actually building the itinerary around it, which is exactly the kind of downstream effect Japan, Worked Out plans for.

Bottom line

For most American visitors, aim for late March–April for cherry blossoms or October–November for fall color — and dodge Golden Week, Obon, New Year, the rainy season, and peak August heat. That said, every season has its rewards, from winter onsen to summer festivals, so the "right" time ultimately depends on what you want to see. Once you've picked your season, the next step is shaping the route.

title: Cherry Blossom Season in Japan: When to Go and What It Costs
content:
Cherry blossom season is the single most requested time to visit Japan, and also the hardest to plan, because the thing you are travelling for does not keep a schedule. The bloom moves north across the country over several weeks, but in any one city it lasts about a week. This guide covers where the blossom lands and when, what the season does to what you pay, and how to book around a date that nobody can guarantee.

When the blossom actually arrives

Cherry blossom reaches full bloom in Kyushu in late March, in Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka from late March into the first days of April — most often somewhere around 28 March to 5 April — in Tohoku in mid to late April, and in Hokkaido from late April into early May. The pattern moves south to north and from low ground upward.

The rough regional timetable

Working from that gradient, a first trip usually targets the Tokyo–Kyoto corridor in the first days of April. Both cities sit in the same broad window, and they are close enough that a week spanning the turn of the month gives you a real chance in at least one of them. Travelling further north buys you a second attempt: if Tokyo has already dropped its petals, Tohoku is often still a fortnight away from opening.

Why nobody can promise you a date

Bloom timing depends on the winter that preceded it, and a warm February can pull the opening forward by a week. The Japan Meteorological Agency stopped issuing the official forecast in 2010, and private forecasters now publish the projections quoted everywhere. Those forecasts are useful from February onward — long after you needed to book flights and rooms. You are booking a window, not an event.

What the season does to what you pay

Bloom season is Japan's most expensive domestic travel period outside the New Year holiday. Accommodation in central Kyoto and Tokyo rises sharply for the same rooms, reserved seats on the fast trains fill early, and the better-regarded inns stop taking new bookings months out. The airfare from the US rises too, though less dramatically than the lodging.

How far ahead to book

Rooms in Kyoto and central Tokyo for the bloom window are commonly booked around six months ahead, and the well-regarded traditional inns go earlier still. That is the uncomfortable part of the timing problem: the booking deadline falls months before any forecast exists. Most people resolve it by choosing the first week of April, accepting the odds, and booking something cancellable.

If your dates are fixed by work or school, plan a trip you would enjoy regardless and treat the blossom as a bonus. A first trip built entirely around one week of flowers disappoints when the flowers run early.

Where the crowds actually are

Crowding in Tokyo and Kyoto during the roughly one-week bloom window concentrates in a small number of famous places rather than spreading evenly. The named parks, the photogenic riverside paths and the temple gardens that appear in every forecast article absorb enormous numbers of people, while ordinary neighbourhood streets a few minutes away carry the same trees with a fraction of the crowd.

Japan treats blossom viewing as a social occasion rather than a spectator sport, which is why the busiest spots stay busy from morning until well after dark. Early morning is the reliable answer at the famous sites — as is simply walking, since residential streets, campuses and canal banks carry the same trees and attract almost nobody.

The three ways people actually play it

Given a booking deadline roughly six months out and a bloom forecast that does not appear until February, travellers to Japan converge on three strategies: book the first days of April and accept the odds, travel south to north and take two chances, or book April for the season and treat the flowers as luck. It is worth choosing between them deliberately rather than drifting into one.

Book the first week of April and accept the odds

The most common approach: the Tokyo-Kyoto corridor most often reaches full bloom around the turn of the month, so a week straddling it has a genuine chance. The cost is peak-season prices paid for a probability, and a warm February leaves you late with nothing but green.

Aim north and follow it

Because the bloom climbs the country over several weeks, a trip that starts in the south and moves north converts a single window into several. Arriving in Kyoto in early April and reaching Tohoku a fortnight later means two separate chances rather than one. The trade-off is that you are committing to a lot of ground, which is a real constraint on a first trip where the cities themselves deserve time.

Go for the season, not the flower

The third option is to book April for the weather and the long daylight, and treat any blossom as luck. Late April is one of the most pleasant stretches of the Japanese year and noticeably cheaper — until the holiday cluster at the end of the month, which is a different problem entirely.

What "full bloom" actually means

Full bloom, the stage Japanese forecasts call mankai, is a specific point rather than a general condition, and the gap between the first flowers opening and the trees being fully out is usually several days. Forecasts quote both the opening date and the full-bloom date for each city, and the second is the one worth planning around — a tree at thirty per cent is a tree with some flowers on it, not the thing people travel for.

The end is quicker than the beginning. Once full bloom passes, a single day of rain or wind can strip a street, which is why advice to build in slack at the front of the window is better than assuming you can catch up at the back.

The alternative nobody mentions

Autumn, which peaks in Kyoto through the second half of November, is Japan's other great season and for a first trip arguably the easier one. Colour holds for weeks rather than days, the weather is more settled, and while it is busy it does not carry bloom season's compressed desperation. If you want Japan at its most beautiful and your dates are flexible, the case for choosing a season deliberately is worth reading before you commit to spring.

Late April is also worth knowing about, once the blossom has passed the main cities. The weather is excellent, prices ease, and the country is green rather than pink — right up until the holiday cluster at the end of the month, which is a different problem entirely.

What the blossom decision is really attached to

Notice what the bloom window has quietly done. A one-week target in Tokyo and Kyoto sets a booking deadline six months out, which fixes how far ahead you commit to rooms, which constrains which cities you can base yourself in, which changes how much of the country you can reach. Chasing the blossom is not a standalone preference — it decides four or five other things, six months before you travel.

That chain is where first trips come apart, usually not because any single decision was wrong but because they were each made separately. Working out how the timing, the bases and the routing between them fit together is what Japan, Worked Out is built to do.

title: Golden Week in Japan: What Closes and What It Costs
content:
Golden Week is the cluster of public holidays at the turn of April into May, and it is the period most often flagged as one to avoid. That advice is broadly right but rarely explained, which leaves travellers either cancelling a workable trip or walking into a week they were not prepared for. Here is what actually closes, what is simply full, and what to do if your dates are fixed.

Which days Golden Week actually covers

Golden Week is built from four national holidays: Showa Day on 29 April, Constitution Day on 3 May, Greenery Day on 4 May and Children's Day on 5 May. Those four dates are fixed in law. How long the resulting run of days lasts is not fixed — it depends entirely on which weekdays those dates land on in a given year.

Why the length changes every year

Japan applies a substitute holiday rule: when a national holiday falls on a Sunday, the next weekday that is not already a holiday becomes a holiday instead. A single working day sandwiched between two holidays also becomes one. In some years those rules knit the whole stretch from 29 April into a continuous break; in others the run is broken by two ordinary working days in the middle.

The practical instruction is to check the actual dates for your year rather than trusting any article that quotes a fixed span. The holidays are stable; the shape of the week is not.

What genuinely closes

Closures during Golden Week are narrower than most travellers expect. Major museums, big temples and shrines, department stores, and the large restaurant groups stay open and are extremely busy. What closes is the smaller layer: family-run restaurants, independent shops, small workshops and some local businesses, which take the break precisely because everyone else is off.

Government offices and banks close on the holidays themselves. That matters less than it once did, but it is worth not scheduling anything administrative into the week.

What it does to prices and seats

Golden Week moves the entire country at once, and the effect on transport and lodging is the real reason to plan around it. Reserved seats on the fast trains sell out well in advance on the main corridors, domestic flights fill, and accommodation prices in the popular cities rise sharply for the same rooms you could have had cheaply a fortnight earlier.

The part that surprises Americans

This is domestic travel, not international tourism. The crowds are Japanese families going home or taking their one reliable block of annual leave, which means the pressure lands hardest on routes and towns that are otherwise quiet. A rural hot-spring town can be harder to book than Tokyo.

It also means the crowding is front-loaded and back-loaded: the heaviest movement is at the start and end of the run, and the middle days are calmer in transit even while the sights stay packed.

Which days inside the run are worst

Pressure during Golden Week is not evenly spread across the days. The heaviest movement falls at the two ends — the outbound surge as the run begins and the return surge as it closes — because that is when the entire working population is travelling in the same direction at the same time.

The middle days behave differently. Transport eases because most people have already arrived where they are going, while the sights themselves stay packed. For a visitor who has to be in Japan during the run, that asymmetry is the single most useful thing to know: move at the middle, sit still at the ends.

The administrative detail

Banks and government offices close on the holidays themselves, and anything requiring a counter and a human becomes difficult across the run. It matters less than it used to, but it is worth handling anything administrative before the week begins rather than assuming a quiet Tuesday will be available.

What the week is like if you stay

Golden Week in Tokyo or Kyoto is not a write-off, and travellers who have been through it often report it as one of the more memorable stretches of a trip. Parks fill with families, temporary food stalls appear, and the ordinary rhythm of the cities gives way to something closer to a national festival. The crowds are good-natured rather than fraught, and the atmosphere is genuinely different from any other week of the year.

If your dates cannot move

A Golden Week trip is entirely workable if you accept two constraints. Book everything early — rooms and any reserved long-distance seats, months ahead rather than weeks. And stay put: this is the wrong week to be relocating between cities every second day, because the moving is where the pain concentrates.

Pick one base, use it properly, and take the pressure off by going out early. A city like Tokyo absorbs crowds far better than a small temple town does, simply because there is more of it. The same logic applies to choosing sights: the enormous, famous ones cope; the small, perfect ones do not.

What the timing decision is attached to

Golden Week, built on four fixed holidays between 29 April and 5 May, does not just make Japan busy — it changes what kind of trip is possible. It pushes you toward fewer bases, earlier commitment, bigger cities and larger sights, and it does that whether or not you planned for any of it. The same is true of the August holiday period and, in a different way, of blossom season.

Each of those is usually treated as a separate warning in a separate article. They are really one decision about when to come, which then reshapes the routing, the bases and the booking order underneath it. Working out that chain in advance, rather than discovering it in sequence, is what Japan, Worked Out sets out to do.

title: Japan's Rainy Season and Typhoons: What They Mean for Your Trip
content:
Two weather patterns get Japan's early summer written off in travel advice: the rainy season and the typhoon season. Both are real, and both are routinely described in a way that makes them sound worse than they are. This guide covers when each actually happens, what they do to a trip in practice, and when they are genuinely worth rearranging plans around.

When the rainy season runs

Japan's rainy season runs from roughly early June to mid or late July in the Tokyo and Kyoto regions, and it moves south to north across the country. Okinawa runs from early May to late June; Kyushu and Shikoku from late May or early June into mid-July; the Tokyo and Kyoto regions from roughly early June to mid or late July; and Tohoku later still. Hokkaido is generally considered not to have one at all.

What it actually feels like

The most useful thing to know is that the rainy season is not weeks of continuous rain. In practice it means high humidity with heavy bursts — a downpour that soaks a street and stops, followed by grey warmth or sudden sun. Whole days are lost to rain much less often than the name implies.

What it does reliably deliver is humidity, which matters more for comfort than the rain does. Temples and gardens look extraordinary in wet weather, the moss is at its best, and the famous places are noticeably less crowded. For a traveller willing to carry an umbrella, June is one of the better-value months of the year.

When typhoon season matters

Typhoons are possible in Japan from roughly May through October, with the peak in August and September. Okinawa, Kyushu and Shikoku are the most exposed; direct hits on Tokyo and Kyoto are less common, though disruption to transport from a storm passing nearby is not.

How disruption actually works

Japanese rail operators announce planned suspensions in advance rather than cancelling services as a storm arrives. That practice is unfamiliar to most American travellers and is genuinely reassuring: you usually know the day before that a line will stop running, which gives you time to move a plan rather than being stranded by it.

A typhoon that affects your trip will most likely cost you one day, not a week. The sensible response is to keep a flexible day in the plan and avoid scheduling anything unmissable — a long-distance journey, or the flight home — for the tail end of a trip in early September.

Should you avoid the summer entirely?

Summer in Japan is worth taking on its own terms rather than avoiding outright, and its real problem is heat rather than either weather pattern. August highs in Tokyo and Kyoto run around 33 to 35C with high humidity, and Kyoto's basin geography makes it feel hotter still. That is a genuine constraint on how much walking a day can hold, and it is the reason August itineraries need to be lighter than spring ones.

Set against that, summer carries the festival calendar, long daylight, and the mountains and northern regions at their most pleasant — Hokkaido in August is excellent. Summer is not a season to avoid so much as one to plan differently.

If your dates are fixed in early summer

June and early July are genuinely good months to travel in Japan provided you plan for the humidity: early starts, indoor anchors in the middle of the day, and no assumption that every afternoon will be dry. Prices sit below both peak seasons and the major sights are calmer than at any other point between March and November.

Early summer, month by month

June, July and September differ enough from one another that treating early summer as a single block is misleading. June carries the rainy season and the lowest crowds of the warm half of the year; July turns hot once the rains lift in the middle of the month; September sits at the typhoon peak while the heat finally begins to ease. Each asks for a different kind of itinerary.

June

June carries the rainy season across most of the main island and is, for that reason, one of the quietest and best-value months in the calendar. Gardens are at their most saturated, the famous sites are noticeably calmer, and the temperature is warm rather than punishing. The cost is humidity and an umbrella in the bag every day.

July

July begins wet and ends hot, with the rainy season lifting somewhere in the middle and the serious heat arriving behind it. The second half of the month starts to demand the lighter, slower kind of itinerary that August requires outright.

September

September sits at the peak of the typhoon season while the heat begins to ease, which makes it a month of trade-offs rather than a straightforward improvement on August. The back half is generally more comfortable than the front, and the crowds are lighter than either peak season.

Building a plan that survives a lost day

A Japan trip in August or September should be built to absorb one lost day, because that is the realistic cost of a typhoon passing near Tokyo or Kyoto rather than the week-long disruption travellers fear. Building that slack in costs very little.

The practical version is to avoid scheduling a long-distance journey or anything unmissable on the final days, and to keep one flexible afternoon in reserve rather than filling every slot.

Because suspensions are announced ahead rather than sprung on passengers, the warning usually arrives with enough time to reorder a plan. What it cannot do is create space in an itinerary that had none, which is the real argument for planning early summer more loosely than spring.

Choosing a season on purpose

Weather is only one input into when to visit Japan, and rarely the decisive one — the rainy season's six weeks and the typhoon peak in August and September matter less to most itineraries than the holiday clusters do.

Weather interacts with those clusters, with lodging prices, and with how much ground an itinerary can cover — a choice that cascades into how many bases you use and how far ahead you commit. Comparing the seasons against each other is a more useful exercise than ruling any single month out.

How that timing decision then reshapes the route, the bases and the booking order underneath it is what Japan, Worked Out is built to work through.

title: Obon in Japan: What Changes in Mid-August
content:
Obon is the mid-August observance when families return to their home towns to honour their ancestors, and it produces one of the heaviest domestic travel weeks of the Japanese year. What catches American visitors out is that it is not a public holiday at all — the calendar shows ordinary working days while the country moves. Here is what changes, and what to do about it.

When Obon falls

Obon is observed around 13 to 16 August across most of Japan, though the observance is not a national holiday and the dates are not fixed by law. Some regions, including parts of Tokyo, keep it in mid-July instead, following the older calendar. For a visitor, the mid-August window is the one that matters, because that is when the bulk of the country travels.

Why a non-holiday empties the cities

Most Japanese companies close for several days around Obon even though the state does not require it, which produces the effect of a national holiday without one appearing on any calendar. Because the tradition is about returning to a family home, the movement runs out of the big cities and into the provinces — the opposite direction to a tourist week.

What actually closes

Closures during Obon fall on the small and family-run layer of Japanese business: independent restaurants, neighbourhood shops, small workshops, and family-owned inns whose owners are themselves observing. Larger museums, department stores, chain restaurants and the major temples and shrines generally stay open.

The pattern is inconsistent enough that it is worth checking specific places rather than assuming. A restaurant you were looking forward to may simply be shut for four days with a handwritten note on the door, and that is normal rather than a sign of anything going wrong.

What it does to travel

Obon, across roughly 13 to 16 August, puts enormous pressure on long-distance transport in both directions: out of the cities at the start, back into them at the end. Reserved seats on the fast trains sell out on the main corridors, domestic flights fill, and expressways congest badly. Accommodation tightens most in the provincial towns and hot-spring resorts that are quiet the rest of the year.

Where the pressure is lighter

Central Tokyo and central Kyoto are, unusually, somewhat calmer during Obon than in the weeks either side, because a substantial share of their residents has left. The cities do not empty — inbound visitors are still there — but the domestic layer thins out. If you are staying put in a big city, Obon is more manageable than its reputation suggests.

The difficulty lands on anyone moving between places in the two or three days at each end of the observance. That is the window to avoid for long journeys, rather than the whole period.

What you can see during the observance

Obon is a religious and family occasion rather than a spectacle staged for visitors, and most of it happens privately — graves tended, household altars prepared, relatives gathered. What is public are the neighbourhood dances held on summer evenings across the country, open to anyone who wants to join the circle, and the lanterns set out to guide ancestors home and away again. Encountering one is a matter of being in a neighbourhood at the right hour rather than buying a ticket.

The other August problem

Obon sits inside Japan's hardest month for weather. August highs in Tokyo and Kyoto run around 33 to 35C with high humidity, and Kyoto's basin geography makes it feel worse than the number suggests. Heat is a genuine constraint on how much walking an itinerary can carry, not merely a comfort note — a plan that works in April will not survive August unmodified.

August is also the peak of the typhoon season, which can remove a travel day at short notice. Neither is a reason to cancel a trip that has to happen in August, but both are reasons to build a lighter plan with indoor options, early starts and long afternoon breaks.

The July observance, and why it confuses people

Parts of Japan, including some Tokyo districts, observe Obon in mid-July rather than mid-August, following the older lunar reckoning. The result is that a visitor can encounter Obon decorations and observances in July in one neighbourhood and find nothing unusual a few train stops away.

The July observance does not produce the national travel surge, which is what makes the August window the one that matters for planning. If you are in Tokyo in mid-July and notice lanterns going up, that is the local calendar rather than a sign that the country is about to move.

Reading the direction of the crowd

Obon travel runs out of Tokyo, Osaka and the other major cities and into the provinces, which is the reverse of almost every other busy period and the reason the usual advice does not apply cleanly. A tourist week concentrates people in Tokyo and Kyoto; Obon disperses residents from them toward home towns, hot-spring resorts and rural districts.

For a visitor, that inversion is worth using rather than fighting. A city-based few days across the observance can be easier than the weeks either side, while a plan built around small provincial towns runs straight into the heaviest demand of the year for exactly the kind of accommodation those towns have least of.

Travelling through it deliberately

Obon, in the middle four days of August, is workable if you treat it as a fixed feature of the map rather than a surprise. Book long-distance travel and rooms well ahead, avoid moving cities in the peak days at either end, and expect small restaurants to be closed.

Choosing when to come is one of the decisions that quietly reshapes everything else about a first trip, which Japan, Worked Out works through in order.

If your dates are flexible and August is not fixed, avoid the few days right around Obon itself — roughly the 10th to the 19th — and either half of the month works; September is easier than all of August once the worst of the heat begins to break.
