title: Winter in Japan: Snow, Onsen and the Quiet Season
content:
Winter is the season most first-time visitors skip, and the one that rewards them most if they do not. Outside a single fortnight around the New Year, it is the quietest and cheapest stretch of the Japanese year, with clear skies and short queues at places that are impossible in spring. This guide covers where the snow actually falls, what the cities are like in the cold, and the one period to plan around.

Where the snow actually is

Reliable snow in Japan falls in Hokkaido, in Tohoku, and along the Japan Sea side of the main island — Niigata, Toyama and Nagano — broadly from December through March. Tokyo and Kyoto get very little. Kyoto snow is an occasional event that photographs beautifully and lasts a morning, not a season you can book.

The expectation worth correcting

A great many people book Kyoto in January expecting the temples under snow they have seen photographed. Those photographs are real and they are rare, taken on a handful of mornings a year. If snow is the point of the trip, the Japan Sea side and the north deliver it reliably and the old capital does not.

What Kyoto does deliver in winter is cold, dry, bright weather and its famous sites at a fraction of their usual density — which is arguably the better prize.

Why the onsen makes sense now

A Japanese hot spring is a year-round institution, but sitting in an outdoor bath at around 40C while snow falls on the surrounding rocks is the version everyone pictures, and winter is when it exists. Onsen towns in the snow country run through the coldest months and are the single strongest argument for a winter trip.

Winter is also when the traditional inns are least booked outside the holiday period, which means the rooms that are impossible to get in November are available and cheaper. If a night at a traditional inn is on the list, this is the season to do it.

What the cities are like

Tokyo and Kyoto in January and February are cold, dry and unusually clear — the winter air gives the best long views of the year, including the days when Mount Fuji is visible from Tokyo. Daylight is short, so plan around a 4:30 sunset rather than fighting it, and build the evening into the day deliberately.

The practical trade-offs

Buildings are heated unevenly by American standards, and older accommodation can be genuinely cold in the corridors even when rooms are warm. Layers matter more than a heavy coat, because you will move between icy streets and overheated trains repeatedly in a day.

Against that: no queues worth the name, restaurants that take walk-ins, and lodging prices below every other season. For a traveller who cares more about seeing places properly than about photographing them at their most colourful, that is a strong trade.

The fortnight to plan around

The New Year period, roughly 29 December to 3 or 4 January, is Japan's most significant closure window and the exception to everything above. Many independent restaurants, small shops, museums and offices close for several consecutive days, department stores typically close on 1 January, and shrines are extremely busy with the first-visit tradition.

This is the closure that catches Americans out most often, because late December reads as an ordinary travel window from the US and the calendar gives no warning. A trip either side of it is excellent. A trip through the middle of it is a different and much more restricted experience.

Winter against the seasons everyone books

Winter is best understood against cherry blossom season and the autumn foliage weeks, because those are what it is competing with in most people's plans. Spring and late autumn offer the spectacle; winter offers access. The same temple that takes forty minutes of queueing in November is walked into in January.

The trade is clear once stated plainly. You give up the colour, the long evenings and the festival atmosphere. You gain the rooms, the prices, the quiet, and the clarity in the air. For a first trip where the point is to see the country rather than photograph one week of it, that trade is better than its reputation.

What to eat in the cold

Japanese winter food is a genuine reason to come rather than a consolation. Hot-pot cooking at the table is at its best in the coldest months, ramen is a different proposition in freezing weather, and the winter seafood season on the Japan Sea coast is the one most prized domestically. Convenience stores switch to hot counters, and the steamed buns and simmered snacks that appear are a small daily pleasure.

Restaurants are also simply available. The places that require a month's notice in spring take walk-ins in February, which changes what a food-focused trip can realistically include.

Skiing, briefly

Japan's ski regions in Hokkaido and Nagano are genuinely world-class and run on their own economics — they are the one part of the country that is expensive and busy in winter. If skiing is the trip, it is a different plan from the one this article describes. If it is not, avoid the resort towns at peak weekends and the rest of the north is empty.

Choosing winter on purpose

Winter, running December through March, is the clearest example of a season that changes what kind of trip is possible rather than simply changing the weather. It opens the traditional inns, closes the New Year fortnight, shortens the usable day, and makes the famous cities navigable in a way they are not for eight months of the year. Japan, Worked Out works through how a timing choice like that reshapes the route and the booking order underneath it.

If your dates are flexible and you have already been told to come in spring, winter is the contrarian answer worth taking seriously — provided you know exactly which fortnight to avoid.
excerpt: Outside the New Year week, winter is Japan's quietest and cheapest season. Where the snow actually is, why Kyoto probably will not have any, and what the cities are like empty.

title: Japan Etiquette: 10 Things Americans Should Know
content:
Japanese etiquette can feel intimidating from afar, but the essentials are simple, and locals are genuinely gracious with visitors who make an effort. None of this requires memorizing a rulebook — just absorbing a handful of habits that differ from American norms. Get these down and you'll move through Japan comfortably and respectfully, and you'll likely find the social smoothness one of the trip's quiet pleasures. Here are the ones that matter most.

1. Don't tip

Tipping is the big one for Americans. It simply isn't customary anywhere in Japan — not in restaurants, taxis, hotels, or salons. Good service is the standard, included in the price, and leaving extra cash often causes genuine confusion (staff may chase you down to return it). It's not rude to skip the tip; it's the expected norm. Forget the 15–20% reflex entirely.

2. Don't eat while walking

Eating on the go is generally frowned upon. If you buy street food or a snack, the polite move is to stand near the stall or step to the side and finish it there before walking on, rather than wandering down the street eating. The same goes for drinking — pause, enjoy, then continue. (This is part of why the streets stay so clean.)

3. Be quiet on public transit

Trains and subways are notably hushed, even when packed. Keep phone calls off entirely (set your phone to silent, "manner mode"), keep conversations low, and avoid loud music through headphones. It's one of the most noticeable cultural differences for visitors and one of the easiest to honor — just match the calm around you.

4. Queue properly

Japan runs on orderly lines — for trains, buses, elevators, shops, taxis, everything. On train platforms, look for the painted floor markings showing where doors open and line up there, letting passengers off before boarding. Cutting in line is a real faux pas that will draw quiet disapproval. When in doubt, find the end of the line.

5. Take your shoes off indoors

Remove your shoes when entering homes, traditional ryokan inns, some restaurants (especially tatami-floored ones), temple buildings, and certain changing rooms. Your cue is a step up (genkan), a shoe rack, or slippers laid out. Wear the provided slippers on regular floors, switch to the separate toilet slippers in the bathroom (and remember to switch back), and step onto tatami in just socks or bare feet.

6. Dress respectfully at temples and shrines

Japan has no strict everyday dress code, and casual clothing is fine almost everywhere. But at temples and shrines, lean a little more conservative — covered shoulders and avoiding very revealing clothing shows respect at these sacred, active places of worship. You don't need to cover up dramatically; just be mindful. This applies a step further at a ryokan's onsen (hot spring bath), where a firmer rule shows up: most onsen still refuse entry to visitors with visible tattoos, though some now offer cover-up stickers or private baths as a workaround — worth confirming with a specific property before you book, which Japan, Worked Out covers alongside choosing a ryokan in the first place.

7. Handle cards and money with both hands

When paying, you'll usually see a small tray at the register for your cash or card, rather than handing it directly to the cashier — place it there. More broadly, using both hands to give and receive money, cards, gifts, and especially business cards (meishi) is a sign of politeness and attentiveness. Receiving a business card with both hands and a moment's respectful look is good manners in any semi-formal setting.

8. Bow when greeting

A slight bow is the standard greeting and a sign of thanks or respect. As a visitor you don't need to get the angles or depth perfect — a small, sincere nod of the head is warmly received and appreciated. You'll find yourself naturally bowing back to staff and others within a day. A handshake isn't expected, though some may offer one to foreigners.

9. Carry your trash

Public trash cans are surprisingly rare on the streets (a legacy of past security concerns), yet the streets are spotless — because the norm is to carry your garbage with you until you find a bin (often by convenience stores or vending machines) or get back to your hotel. Pack a small bag for wrappers, bottles, and receipts, and you'll be set. Don't litter, ever.

10. Mind the small courtesies

A few final habits: don't blow your nose loudly in public (step away or sniff discreetly), don't point at people (gesture with an open hand), avoid loud or boisterous behavior in public, and don't stick chopsticks upright in rice or pass food chopstick-to-chopstick at meals. When unsure, simply observe what those around you are doing and follow suit — attentiveness is itself the core courtesy.

Bottom line

None of this is hard, and locals sincerely appreciate the effort even when you don't get everything perfect. Master these ten habits — above all, don't tip, stay quiet on trains, queue politely, and carry your trash — and you'll move through Japan comfortably, respectfully, and like a considerate guest. The effort is repaid many times over in the warmth you'll encounter.
